shelves.title: Prevention: stopping disease before it starts
shelves.question: What can be prevented — heart attacks, strokes, diabetes, cancer, fractures, infections — and what does the evidence say actually works?
shelves.balance: Prevention is where this library’s evidence is strongest and strangest. Some of it is medicine’s greatest hits: folic acid prevents neural tube defects; statins and blood-pressure treatment prevent heart attacks and strokes; HPV vaccination prevents cervical cancer. Some of it failed its trials: vitamin E did not prevent prostate cancer, beta-carotene caused lung cancer in smokers, and annual vitamin D mega-doses caused falls. This shelf lists every prevention question in the library, grouped by what you are trying to prevent — the wins, the nulls, and the backfires alike — and points to the shelf where each one’s evidence lives.

shelves.title: Methadone vs buprenorphine for opioid use disorder: being in treatment — on either drug — is where the mortality difference lives
shelves.question: For opioid use disorder, what do methadone and buprenorphine each do to the risk of dying — and how do they compare with each other?
shelves.mesh: Opioid-Related Disorders · Opiate Substitution Treatment · Methadone · Buprenorphine · Drug Overdose · Humans
shelves.balance: The mortality evidence is observational — cohorts, not randomized mortality trials — and the stamp carries that on its face. Within that fence, the signal is large and consistent: pooled death rates in treatment run at roughly a third of the rates out of treatment for methadone and under half for buprenorphine, for overdose deaths as for all deaths, with the danger concentrated in methadone's first four weeks and in the weeks after leaving either drug. The between-drug question is narrower than it looks: flexible-dose methadone retains people better than flexible-dose buprenorphine (RR 0.83, relative), and at adequate fixed doses the retention gap closes — but no randomized trial compares the two drugs on mortality, and the cohort rates cannot be read as a head-to-head. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Mortality in and out of opioid substitution treatment (Sordo 2017, BMJ): death rates roughly threefold lower while in treatment — observational cohorts, stated as such
cards.summary: 19 prospective or retrospective cohorts — 122,885 people treated with methadone (follow-up 1.3–13.9 years) and 15,831 with buprenorphine (1.1–4.5 years). Pooled all-cause mortality was 11.3 per 1,000 person-years in methadone treatment vs 36.1 out of treatment (unadjusted out-to-in rate ratio 3.20 [2.65–3.86], relative) and 4.3 in vs 9.5 out of buprenorphine treatment (rate ratio 2.20 [1.34–3.61], relative). Overdose mortality: 2.6 in vs 12.7 out per 1,000 person-years on methadone (rate ratio 4.80 [2.90–7.96], relative) and 1.4 in vs 4.6 out on buprenorphine . Risk spiked in the first four weeks of methadone induction and in the weeks just after leaving either treatment.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies (Sordo 2017, BMJ). No registry ID applies — this is a meta-analysis of cohorts, not a trial. The record prints no pooled mean age or sex mix for the cohorts, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 19 eligible cohorts: 122,885 people treated with methadone and 15,831 treated with buprenorphine, followed 1.1–13.9 years across the cohorts.
cards.result: Pooled all-cause mortality rates were 11.3 and 36.1 per 1000 person-years in and out of methadone treatment (unadjusted out-to-in rate ratio 3.20, 95% CI 2.65 to 3.86) and 4.3 and 9.5 in and out of buprenorphine treatment (2.20, 1.34 to 3.61). Overdose mortality rates were 2.6 and 12.7 per 1000 person-years in and out of methadone treatment (rate ratio 4.80, 2.90 to 7.96) and 1.4 and 4.6 in and out of buprenorphine treatment. All-cause mortality dropped sharply over the first four weeks of methadone treatment, remained stable during buprenorphine treatment, and rose after leaving treatment with either drug.
cards.watchOut: This is observational evidence — cohorts, not randomized mortality trials — and the authors themselves flag confounding and selection bias: people who stay in treatment differ from people who leave it. The in-treatment rates also differ between the drugs (11.3 vs 4.3 per 1000 person-years) because the methadone and buprenorphine cohorts were different populations, not because one drug was randomized against the other — this card does not support a between-drug mortality claim. The induction and post-cessation windows are the dangerous weeks for both drugs.
cards.source: Sordo L et al. Mortality risk during and after opioid substitution treatment: systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies. BMJ. 2017;357:j1550. PMID 28446428. DOI 10.1136/bmj.j1550

cards.headline: Retention: methadone vs buprenorphine (Mattick 2014, Cochrane): flexible-dose methadone retains better; at adequate fixed doses the gap narrows
cards.summary: 31 randomized trials, 5,430 participants. With flexible dosing adjusted to need, buprenorphine retained fewer participants than methadone — RR 0.83 [0.72–0.95] (relative; 5 studies, 788 participants, high-quality evidence). At fixed medium doses (buprenorphine 7–15 mg vs methadone 40–85 mg) retention did not differ (RR 0.87 [0.69–1.10]), and at fixed high doses (≥16 mg vs ≥85 mg) it did not differ either (RR 0.79 [0.20–3.16]). Among those retained, suppression of illicit opioid use did not differ between the drugs. Low fixed-dose buprenorphine (2–6 mg) retained worse than low-dose methadone (RR 0.67 [0.52–0.87]).
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of 31 randomized controlled trials (Mattick 2014). No registry ID applies to the review itself. The record does not print a pooled mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 31 trials, 5,430 participants with opioid dependence, comparing buprenorphine maintenance with placebo or with methadone maintenance.
cards.result: There is high quality of evidence that buprenorphine in flexible doses was less effective than methadone in retaining participants (5 studies, 788 participants, RR 0.83; 95% CI 0.72 to 0.95). For those retained, no difference was observed in suppression of opioid use by urinalysis (8 studies, 1027 participants, SMD −0.11; 95% CI −0.23 to 0.02). In fixed-dose studies, low-dose methadone (≤40 mg) retained better than low-dose buprenorphine (2–6 mg) (RR 0.67; 95% CI 0.52 to 0.87), but there was no difference at medium doses (RR 0.87; 95% CI 0.69 to 1.10) or high doses (RR 0.79; 95% CI 0.20 to 3.16). Only high-dose buprenorphine (≥16 mg) suppressed illicit opioid use better than placebo on urinalysis.
cards.watchOut: Retention is a process outcome, not mortality — its link to the survival difference on Card 1 is inference, though it is the mechanism the cohort data point to. Flexible-dose comparisons may partly reflect dosing culture (methadone titrated up, buprenorphine capped) rather than the molecules alone. Few trials reported adverse events; the one consistent difference was more sedation with methadone.

shelves.title: Extended-release naltrexone vs buprenorphine (X:BOT): equivalent once started — harder to start
shelves.question: A monthly naltrexone injection against daily buprenorphine: which keeps people off opioids — and what does the answer depend on?
shelves.mesh: Opioid-Related Disorders · Naltrexone · Buprenorphine, Naloxone Drug Combination · Delayed-Action Preparations · Humans
shelves.balance: One trial, two honest answers, and both are stamped. As offered (intention-to-treat), buprenorphine-naloxone produced fewer relapses over 24 weeks (57% vs 65%; HR 1.36, relative) — a difference manufactured almost entirely at the front door, where 94% of patients successfully started buprenorphine against 72% for the injection, which demands an opioid-free interval first. Once successfully inducted, relapse did not differ (per-protocol, P=0.44), and the Norwegian trial — where induction was inpatient and already complete — found XR-naltrexone noninferior on retention and urine tests over 12 weeks. Mortality in X:BOT was five fatal overdoses in total (2 XR-NTX, 3 BUP-NX); neither trial was powered for death. The practical reading: the choice between these drugs is mostly a choice about which induction problem your setting can solve. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: X:BOT (Lee 2018, Lancet): as offered, buprenorphine wins on relapse — because a quarter of the naltrexone group never got started
cards.summary: 570 adults with DSM-5 opioid use disorder at eight US inpatient services, randomized to monthly XR-naltrexone injections or daily buprenorphine-naloxone film for 24 weeks. Induction succeeded in 72% (204/283) on XR-NTX vs 94% (270/287) on BUP-NX (P<0.0001). Intention-to-treat relapse: 65% (185/283) vs 57% (163/287) — HR 1.36 [1.10–1.68], relative — and almost all of that difference was early relapse in the XR-NTX induction failures (89% of them relapsed). Among the 474 successfully inducted (per-protocol), relapse was similar (P=0.44) ; the record does not state the per-protocol relapse percentages, so none are carded. Five fatal overdoses occurred — 2 on XR-NTX and 3 on BUP-NX — and overdose events otherwise did not differ.
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomized comparative-effectiveness trial (X:BOT; Lee 2018, Lancet). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT02032433.
cards.people: 570 participants aged 18 or older with DSM-5 opioid use disorder who had used non-prescribed opioids in the past 30 days, recruited at eight US community-based inpatient services. The record does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: Fewer participants successfully initiated XR-NTX (204 [72%] of 283) than BUP-NX (270 [94%] of 287; P<0.0001). In the intention-to-treat population, 24-week relapse events were greater for XR-NTX (185 [65%] of 283) than for BUP-NX (163 [57%] of 287; HR 1.36, 95% CI 1.10–1.68), most or all of this difference accounted for by early relapse in nearly all (70 [89%] of 79) XR-NTX induction failures. Among participants successfully inducted (per-protocol, n=474), 24-week relapse events were similar across groups (P=0.44). Five fatal overdoses occurred (two XR-NTX, three BUP-NX); other treatment-emergent adverse events, including overdose, did not differ except mild-to-moderate injection-site reactions with XR-NTX.
cards.watchOut: Both readings of this trial are true and they answer different questions: as a treatment you offer a patient today, buprenorphine wins because induction onto naltrexone requires an opioid-free interval many patients do not survive; as pharmacology in a patient already inducted, the two are equivalent within this trial's precision. The trial was open-label, and 24 weeks is short for a chronic relapsing condition.
cards.source: Lee JD et al. Comparative effectiveness of extended-release naltrexone versus buprenorphine-naloxone for opioid relapse prevention (X:BOT): a multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2018;391(10118):309–318. PMID 29150198. NCT02032433 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(17)32812-X

cards.headline: The Norwegian replication (Tanum 2017, JAMA Psychiatry): with inpatient detox already done, XR-naltrexone was noninferior to buprenorphine-naloxone
cards.summary: 159 newly detoxified adults (mean age 36 years; 27.7% women) at five Norwegian addiction clinics, randomized to XR-naltrexone 380 mg every four weeks or daily buprenorphine-naloxone 4–24 mg for 12 weeks. Retention was noninferior (difference −0.1 [−0.2 to 0.1]; mean time in treatment 69.3 vs 63.7 days), the proportion of opioid-negative urine tests was noninferior (0.9 vs 0.8), and days of heroin and other illicit opioid use were lower on XR-naltrexone in superiority analyses. 105 (66.0%) completed the trial.
cards.type: 12-week, multicenter, outpatient, open-label randomized noninferiority trial (Tanum 2017, JAMA Psychiatry). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01717963.
cards.people: Of 232 individuals assessed, 159 were randomized (80 XR-naltrexone, 79 buprenorphine-naloxone); mean (SD) age 36 (8.6) years, 44 (27.7%) women; 105 (66.0%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Retention in the extended-release naltrexone group was noninferior to the buprenorphine-naloxone group (difference, −0.1; 95% CI, −0.2 to 0.1; P=.04), with mean (SD) time in treatment of 69.3 (25.9) and 63.7 (29.9) days. XR-naltrexone showed noninferiority on the proportion of opioid-negative urine drug tests (mean [SD] 0.9 [0.3] vs 0.8 [0.4]; P<.001 for noninferiority) and on use of heroin (mean difference, −3.2; 95% CI, −4.9 to −1.5) and other illicit opioids (−2.7; −4.6 to −0.9). No significant differences were found for most other illicit substance use.
cards.watchOut: This trial answers the induction question by removing it: everyone entered already detoxified, in a system where that step is inpatient — exactly the population X:BOT's per-protocol analysis describes. It does not show that XR-naltrexone can be started as easily in ordinary outpatient practice, and 12 weeks is shorter than X:BOT's 24. Open-label, like X:BOT.

JAMA Psychiatry. 2017;74(12):1197–1205. PMID 29049469. NCT01717963 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2017.3206

shelves.title: Medicines for alcohol use disorder: modest absolute effects — NNTs of 12 to 20 — and one drug that only works watched
shelves.question: Which medicines actually reduce drinking in alcohol use disorder, how large are the effects in absolute terms, and where does disulfiram fit?
shelves.mesh: Alcohol-Related Disorders · Alcoholism · Acamprosate · Naltrexone · Disulfiram · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Humans
shelves.balance: Two medicines have replicated, placebo-controlled support with small absolute effects: acamprosate (NNT 12 to prevent return to any drinking) and oral naltrexone 50 mg (NNT 20 for any drinking, NNT 12 for heavy drinking) — printed as NNTs because the percentages alone flatter them. The largest single trial complicates both stories: COMBINE found naltrexone plus simple medical management sufficient, intensive behavioral therapy and acamprosate adding nothing measurable, and its acamprosate arm flatly null against the meta-analysis's positive pool. Disulfiram is carded at its true grade: null for abstinence in the blinded VA trial, with any real benefit confined to supervised administration — a claim about watching, not about the molecule. None of these trials establishes a mortality benefit, and the shelf claims none. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: The meta-analysis (Jonas 2014, JAMA): acamprosate and oral naltrexone work — with numbers needed to treat of 12 to 20
cards.summary: 122 randomized trials and 1 cohort study, 22,803 outpatients with alcohol use disorders. Acamprosate: NNT 12 [8–26] to prevent return to any drinking (risk difference −0.09). Oral naltrexone 50 mg/day: NNT 20 [11–500] to prevent return to any drinking (risk difference −0.05) and NNT 12 [8–26] to prevent return to heavy drinking . Head-to-head, acamprosate and naltrexone did not differ significantly. Injectable naltrexone showed no association with return to any or heavy drinking. Withdrawal from trials for adverse events: NNH 48 for naltrexone. The record's outcomes are drinking outcomes — it reports no pooled mortality benefit, and none is claimed on this shelf.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Jonas 2014, JAMA) of randomized trials of at least 12 weeks. No registry ID applies to the review itself. The record does not print a pooled mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 122 RCTs and 1 cohort study, 22,803 participants in total; most trials assessed acamprosate (27 studies, n=7,519), naltrexone (53 studies, n=9,140), or both.
cards.result: The NNT to prevent return to any drinking was 12 (95% CI, 8 to 26; RD −0.09) for acamprosate and 20 (95% CI, 11 to 500; RD −0.05) for oral naltrexone (50 mg/d). The NNT to prevent return to heavy drinking was 12 (95% CI, 8 to 26; RD −0.09) for oral naltrexone (50 mg/d). Meta-analyses comparing acamprosate with naltrexone found no statistically significant difference for return to any drinking (RD 0.02) or heavy drinking (RD 0.01). For injectable naltrexone, meta-analyses found no association with return to any drinking or return to heavy drinking, but an association with reduction in heavy drinking days (WMD −4.6%). NNH for withdrawal from trials due to adverse events was 48 for naltrexone; risk was not significantly increased for acamprosate.
cards.watchOut: These are real but small absolute effects — one extra patient abstinent or not-heavy-drinking for every 12 to 20 treated — on drinking outcomes, not on death, injury, or liver outcomes, which the trials largely did not measure. Most of the evidence is against placebo, with the two drugs rarely compared directly.
cards.source: Jonas DE et al. Pharmacotherapy for adults with alcohol use disorders in outpatient settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA. 2014;311(18):1889–1900. PMID 24825644. DOI 10.1001/jama.2014.3628

cards.headline: COMBINE (Anton 2006, JAMA): naltrexone plus medical management was enough — adding intensive behavioral therapy, or acamprosate, added nothing
cards.summary: 1,383 recently abstinent adults with alcohol dependence (median age 44 years) at 11 US academic sites, in eight pill-and-therapy combinations plus a therapy-only group, for 16 weeks. Percent days abstinent: 80.6% on naltrexone + medical management, 79.2% on CBI + medical management + placebo, 77.1% on both — vs 75.1% on placebo + medical management alone . Naltrexone reduced the risk of a heavy drinking day (HR 0.72 [0.53–0.98], relative). Acamprosate showed no significant effect on drinking, alone or in any combination. CBI without pills or medical management did worst (66.6% days abstinent). One year after treatment, the between-group effects were similar but no longer significant.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (the COMBINE study; Anton 2006, JAMA — the record's journal is JAMA, not NEJM). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT00006206.
cards.people: 1,383 recently alcohol-abstinent volunteers with DSM-IV primary alcohol dependence from 11 US academic sites; median age 44 years. The record does not print a sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: During treatment, patients receiving naltrexone plus medical management (n=302), CBI plus medical management and placebos (n=305), or both (n=309) had higher percent days abstinent (80.6, 79.2, and 77.1, respectively) than the 75.1 in those receiving placebos and medical management only (n=305), with a significant naltrexone × behavioral intervention interaction (P=.009). Naltrexone also reduced risk of a heavy drinking day (hazard ratio 0.72; 97.5% CI 0.53–0.98; P=.02). Acamprosate showed no significant effect on drinking versus placebo, by itself or in combination. One year after treatment, between-group effects were similar but no longer significant.
cards.watchOut: COMBINE's acamprosate null sits against Card 1's positive pooled acamprosate result — the shelf prints both: one very large trial found nothing for acamprosate while the meta-analysis of smaller trials found an NNT of 12. Every group, placebo included, cut drinking substantially, which is itself a finding about medical management: brief structured contact plus a pill ritual did much of the work.

cards.headline: Disulfiram (Fuller 1986, JAMA — the VA cooperative study): blinded, it did not produce abstinence; its signal lives in supervised, adherent use
cards.summary: 605 men with alcoholism at VA centers, randomized to disulfiram 250 mg, disulfiram 1 mg (a control for the threat of the reaction), or no disulfiram, all with counseling, followed one year. There were no significant differences among the groups in total abstinence, time to first drink, employment, or social stability — the null appears first. Among patients who drank and completed assessments, the 250-mg group reported fewer drinking days (49.0 vs 75.4 and 86.5). Adherence to the regimen tracked with complete abstinence in all groups — which is the supervision problem in one sentence: disulfiram's effect appears where someone watches it being taken.
cards.type: Controlled, blinded, multicenter randomized trial (VA cooperative study; Fuller 1986, JAMA). The record carries no registry databank entry — the trial predates trial registration — so no registry ID is printed.
cards.people: 605 men randomly assigned to 250 mg disulfiram (202), 1 mg disulfiram (204), or no disulfiram (199), with bimonthly assessments for one year; reports corroborated by relative/friend interviews and blood and urine ethanol analyses.
cards.result: There were no significant differences among the groups in total abstinence, time to first drink, employment, or social stability. Among the patients who drank and had a complete set of assessment interviews, those in the 250-mg group reported significantly fewer drinking days (49.0 ± 8.4) than those in the 1-mg (75.4 ± 11.9) or no-disulfiram (86.5 ± 13.6) groups. There was a significant relationship between adherence to drug regimen and complete abstinence in all groups.
cards.watchOut: The 1-mg arm is the clever part of this design: it separates the pharmacology from the fear of the reaction, and under blinding the fear is what patients cannot verify — so the blinded trial tests the drug nearly stripped of its real-world mechanism. Open-label supervised administration (a spouse, a clinic, a court) is a different intervention from the one trialed here, and its evidence is observational. The drinking-days result is a subgroup of drinkers with complete interviews, printed as such.
cards.source: Fuller RK et al. Disulfiram treatment of alcoholism. A Veterans Administration cooperative study. JAMA. 1986;256(11):1449–1455. PMID 3528541.

shelves.title: Contingency management for stimulant use disorder: the largest psychosocial effect during treatment — durability after the incentives stop is the open question
shelves.question: Paying people, in vouchers or prizes, for verified abstinence: does contingency management work for stimulant use disorder — and for how long?
shelves.mesh: Cocaine-Related Disorders · Behavior Therapy · Psychotherapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Humans
shelves.balance: During treatment, the evidence is as strong as psychosocial evidence gets: across two independent syntheses, contingency management carries the largest effect sizes of any psychosocial approach (Dutra 2008), and in the 157-study cocaine network it was the only category of any kind — drug or therapy — significantly associated with drug-negative tests at end of treatment (OR 2.13, relative). The fence is printed in the title: both syntheses measure outcomes while the incentives are running. Abstinence commonly attenuates after incentives end, and neither card's record quantifies long-term post-incentive abstinence — so durability grades POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, and any program built on this shelf should be read as buying abstinence during the program, with the after-period unproven. The VA's national rollout of contingency management is implementation of this evidence, not additional evidence. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: The meta-analytic spine (Dutra 2008, Am J Psychiatry): contingency management carried the strongest effect of any psychosocial treatment reviewed
cards.summary: 34 well-controlled treatment conditions, 2,340 patients, across cannabis, cocaine, opiate, and polysubstance trials. Psychosocial treatments overall produced moderate effect sizes; the strongest effect was found for contingency management interventions — tangible rewards contingent on verified abstinence. About one-third of participants dropped out of psychosocial treatment before completion, vs 44.6% in control conditions. Effects were largest for cannabis use and smallest for polysubstance use in this analysis.
cards.type: Meta-analysis of well-controlled treatment trials (Dutra 2008, Am J Psychiatry). No registry ID applies to the review itself. The record does not print a pooled mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 34 treatment conditions (5 cannabis, 9 cocaine, 7 opiate, 13 polysubstance) representing 2,340 patients.
cards.result: Overall, controlled trial data suggest psychosocial treatments provide benefits reflecting a moderate effect size. The strongest effect was found for contingency management interventions. Approximately one-third of participants across all psychosocial treatments dropped out before treatment completion, compared with 44.6% for control conditions. Interventions were most efficacious for cannabis use and least efficacious for polysubstance use.
cards.watchOut: The outcomes here are end-of-treatment outcomes. Neither this review nor Card 2's network analysis was built to measure what happens after the incentives stop — the durability question is fenced on the shelf's face rather than answered by these cards. Effect sizes pooled across substances hide the split: contingency management's case is strongest exactly where this shelf aims it, at stimulants.

cards.headline: The network analysis (Bentzley 2021, JAMA Network Open): for cocaine use disorder, contingency management was the only treatment category that beat its comparators on drug-negative tests
cards.summary: 157 studies, 402 treatment groups, 15,842 participants with active cocaine use, comparing 11 treatment categories head-to-head through the network. Only contingency management programs were significantly associated with an increased likelihood of a cocaine-negative urinalysis at end of treatment — OR 2.13 [1.62–2.80], relative — and the association held in all sensitivity analyses. No medication category, and no other psychotherapy category, achieved that. (The brief carried this as a JAMA Psychiatry analysis of stimulant use disorder generally; the record is JAMA Network Open, and its population is cocaine use disorder — the card follows the record.)
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis (Bentzley 2021, JAMA Network Open) of clinical trials published 1995–2017. No registry ID applies to the review itself.
cards.people: 157 studies comprising 402 treatment groups and 15,842 participants; outpatients aged 18 or older with active cocaine use at baseline.
cards.result: Only contingency management programs were significantly associated with an increased likelihood of having a negative test result for the presence of cocaine metabolites (OR 2.13; 95% CI 1.62–2.80), and this association remained significant in all sensitivity analyses. Treatments were clustered into 11 categories, including psychotherapy, placebo, opioids, psychostimulants, anticonvulsants, dopamine agonists, antidepressants, and antipsychotics; no other category was significantly associated with the outcome.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is a urine test at the end of treatment — while incentives are still running. This analysis cannot speak to abstinence months after the last voucher, and the shelf does not let it. Trials were mostly US outpatient studies in people actively using cocaine; methamphetamine-specific trial networks are thinner, and this shelf's stimulant claim leans on the cocaine data plus Dutra's cross-substance review.

shelves.title: Community naloxone distribution: stamped LIKELY by developer override, over observational evidence printed at its true grade
shelves.question: Does putting naloxone kits and overdose training into the hands of bystanders lower a community's overdose death rate?
shelves.mesh: Drug Overdose · Naloxone · Harm Reduction · Health Education · Massachusetts · Humans
shelves.balance: The evidence, graded on its own: one interrupted time-series study of 19 Massachusetts communities found overdose death rates lower where overdose-education-and-naloxone programs were implemented, with a dose-response by implementation intensity (adjusted rate ratios 0.73 low, 0.54 high, both relative and ecological) and 327 reported rescues by trained bystanders. That is the whole spine — no randomized trials exist, and the developer's own observational-evidence floor treats ratios between 0.5 and 2.0 as not solid, which covers the low-implementation estimate entirely. The LIKELY stamp is therefore explicitly the developer's judgment — weighing the dose-response, the rescues, the mechanism (naloxone reverses opioid overdose; that pharmacology is not in doubt), and the absence of a plausible harm — laid over evidence that on this library's usual rules would grade lower. Both facts stay printed. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Massachusetts communities (Walley 2013, BMJ): overdose deaths lower where bystander naloxone programs ran — with a dose-response by implementation intensity
cards.summary: Interrupted time-series analysis of 19 Massachusetts communities, 2002–2009. Programs trained 2,912 potential bystanders, who reported 327 rescues . Against communities with no implementation, adjusted overdose-death rate ratios were 0.73 [0.57–0.91] for low implementation (1–100 enrollments per 100,000) and 0.54 [0.39–0.76] for high implementation (>100 per 100,000) — relative, ecological, observational. Rates of acute-care hospital utilization did not differ significantly.
cards.type: Interrupted time-series analysis (Walley 2013, BMJ) — observational, community-level (ecological) data; no randomized trial of community naloxone distribution exists. No registry ID applies. The record does not print an individual-level age or sex mix — the units are communities — so none is stated here.
cards.people: 19 Massachusetts communities with at least five fatal opioid overdoses in each of the years 2004–2006; OEND implemented among people at risk of overdose, agency staff, family, and friends.
cards.result: Both community-year strata with 1–100 enrollments per 100,000 population (adjusted rate ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.91) and strata with greater than 100 enrollments per 100,000 (0.54, 0.39 to 0.76) had significantly reduced adjusted rate ratios for opioid overdose death compared with communities with no implementation. Differences in rates of acute care hospital utilization were not significant. OEND programs trained 2912 potential bystanders who reported 327 rescues.
cards.watchOut: Every caveat the developer's floor requires is on this card: the design is ecological — communities, not individuals, are the unit — so secular trends, co-interventions, and differences between adopting and non-adopting towns can move these ratios; the low-implementation ratio (0.73) sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library treats as not solid evidence on its own, and even the high-implementation ratio (0.54) only just clears it. There are no randomized trials of community naloxone distribution. The LIKELY stamp on this shelf is the developer's judgment over this evidence, stated as such — not the evidence's own grade.

shelves.title: Esketamine for treatment-resistant depression: one pivotal trial met its primary, two missed — a modest effect with a clinic-visit burden
shelves.question: Does esketamine nasal spray, added to a new oral antidepressant, work for treatment-resistant depression — across the whole pivotal trial set, not just the winner?
shelves.mesh: Depressive Disorder, Treatment-Resistant · Ketamine · Antidepressive Agents · Administration, Intranasal · Double-Blind Method · Humans
shelves.balance: The short-term set, carded whole: TRANSFORM-2 (flexible dose) met its primary with a −4.0-point MADRS advantage at 4 weeks; TRANSFORM-1 (fixed dose) missed (P=0.088 at the gatekeeping dose) and TRANSFORM-3 (age 65+) missed (P=0.059). The point estimates barely move across the three — roughly −3 to −4 MADRS points — so the honest dispute is not direction but how much a modest average difference, measured on a subjective scale in trials where dissociation partly unblinds patients, is worth. SUSTAIN-1 shows continuing esketamine delays relapse in patients already selected for responding to it (NNT 4–6), which supports continuation decisions, not starting ones. Against the benefit: dissociation, vertigo, and transient blood-pressure effects around dosing, discontinuation for adverse events of 7% vs 0.9% in TRANSFORM-2, and administration only in a certified clinic under observation (REMS) — a real burden priced into every dose. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: TRANSFORM-2 (Popova 2019): the one pivotal short-term trial that met its primary — MADRS −4.0 points vs active control at day 28
cards.summary: 227 adults with treatment-resistant depression (nonresponse to at least two antidepressants in the current episode) randomized to flexibly dosed esketamine nasal spray (56 or 84 mg twice weekly) plus a newly started oral antidepressant, vs a new antidepressant plus placebo spray. Change in MADRS at day 28 favored esketamine by −4.0 points (95% CI −7.31 to −0.64) , with separation at earlier time points. Discontinuation for adverse events: 7% vs 0.9% . The five most common adverse events — dissociation, nausea, vertigo, dysgeusia, dizziness — were all more frequent on esketamine and generally resolved by 1.5 hours after dosing; the record does not state a dissociation percentage, so none is carded.
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, active-controlled, multicenter trial (TRANSFORM-2; Popova 2019, Am J Psychiatry). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT02418585.
cards.people: 435 patients screened, 227 randomized, 197 completed the 28-day phase; adults with moderate-to-severe nonpsychotic depression and nonresponse to at least two antidepressants in the current episode, one assessed prospectively. The record does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: Change in MADRS score with esketamine plus antidepressant was significantly greater than with antidepressant plus placebo at day 28 (difference of least square means −4.0, SE 1.69, 95% CI −7.31 to −0.64); clinically meaningful improvement was also observed at earlier time points. The five most common adverse events (dissociation, nausea, vertigo, dysgeusia, dizziness) were all more frequent in the esketamine arm; 7% vs 0.9% discontinued study drug because of an adverse event. Adverse events generally appeared shortly after dosing and resolved by 1.5 hours.
cards.watchOut: A −4-point average MADRS difference is a modest group effect — some patients respond dramatically, many do not, and this trial cannot sort them in advance. Dissociation and the other acute effects unblind patients in practice even inside a double-blind trial, which inflates subjective-scale differences by an amount nobody can subtract. Esketamine is given in clinic under observation (the REMS program) — that burden is part of the treatment being graded.

cards.headline: TRANSFORM-1 (Fedgchin 2019): the fixed-dose pivotal trial MISSED its primary endpoint — stated first, as the shelf requires
cards.summary: The primary endpoint was not met. 346 adults with treatment-resistant depression randomized to esketamine 56 mg or 84 mg plus a new oral antidepressant, or placebo spray plus antidepressant, for 4 weeks. Under the prespecified testing sequence, the 84-mg dose had to succeed first: its MADRS difference was −3.2 [−6.88 to 0.45], P=0.088 — not significant — so the 56-mg dose (−4.1 [−7.67 to −0.49], nominal P=0.027) could not be formally tested. Adverse events above 20% on esketamine: nausea, dissociation, dizziness, vertigo, headache.
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, multicenter trial (TRANSFORM-1; Fedgchin 2019, Int J Neuropsychopharmacol). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT02417064.
cards.people: 346 adults with moderate-to-severe depression and nonresponse to at least two antidepressants in the current episode, randomized 1:1:1. The record does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: Statistical significance was not achieved with esketamine 84 mg/antidepressant compared with antidepressant/placebo (LS mean difference −3.2 [95% CI −6.88, 0.45]; P=.088). Although esketamine 56 mg/antidepressant could not be formally tested, the LS mean difference was −4.1 [−7.67, −0.49] (nominal P=.027). The most common (>20%) adverse events for esketamine/antidepressant were nausea, dissociation, dizziness, vertigo, and headache. The authors note the treatment effect for both dose groups exceeded what has been considered clinically meaningful for approved antidepressants versus placebo.
cards.watchOut: A missed primary in a pivotal trial is a missed primary: the nominal 56-mg result is hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory, and this shelf grades the esketamine set as a set — one positive flexible-dose trial, two missed primaries — rather than by its best member. The effect sizes across all three short-term trials are consistently in the −3 to −4 point range; the argument is about reliability and meaning, not direction.

cards.headline: TRANSFORM-3 (Ochs-Ross 2020): in patients 65 and older, the primary endpoint MISSED too — P=0.059
cards.summary: The primary endpoint was not met. Patients aged 65 or older with treatment-resistant depression randomized to flexibly dosed esketamine plus a new oral antidepressant vs antidepressant plus placebo spray. The median-unbiased estimate of the MADRS treatment difference at day 28 was −3.6 [−7.20 to 0.07]; P=0.059 . Subgroup cuts favored ages 65–74 (−4.9, nominal P=0.017) over 75 and older (−0.4, nominal P=0.930) — post-hoc texture, not a rescued primary.
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind trial (TRANSFORM-3; Ochs-Ross 2020, Am J Geriatr Psychiatry). The record carries no registry databank entry, so no registry ID is printed for this card.
cards.people: Patients with treatment-resistant depression aged 65 years or older, randomized 1:1; preplanned analysis by age (65–74 versus 75 and older). The record does not print the randomized total or a sex mix in its abstract, so none is stated here.
cards.result: For the primary endpoint, the median-unbiased estimate of the treatment difference (95% CI) was −3.6 (−7.20, 0.07); weighted combination test P=0.059 — not statistically significant. The adjusted mean difference was −4.9 (nominal P=0.017) for patients 65 to 74 years versus −0.4 (nominal P=0.930) for those 75 years and older, and −6.1 (nominal P=0.006) for depression onset before 55 years versus 3.1 (nominal P=0.407) for onset at 55 or later. Patients who rolled into the long-term open-label study showed continued improvement with four additional weeks of esketamine.
cards.watchOut: Elderly patients are exactly where a rapidly acting option would be most valuable and where this program's evidence is weakest: a near-miss primary, driven by the younger-old subgroup, with the oldest patients showing no separation at all. Subgroup rescues after a missed primary are how false positives are manufactured; the shelf does not perform one.

cards.headline: SUSTAIN-1 (Daly 2019): relapse prevention in a randomized-withdrawal design — in patients already selected for responding to esketamine
cards.summary: 705 adults with treatment-resistant depression entered; after 16 weeks of open esketamine treatment, the 297 who achieved stable remission or stable response were randomized to continue esketamine or switch to placebo spray (oral antidepressant continued in both). Relapse: in stable remitters, 26.7% vs 45.3% (NNT 6; HR 0.49 [0.29–0.84], relative) ; in stable responders, 25.8% vs 57.6% (NNT 4; HR 0.30 [0.16–0.55], relative) . Common adverse events after randomization (20.4%–27.0%): dysgeusia, vertigo, dissociation, somnolence, dizziness. The design is stated in the title and meant: this estimates the value of continuing esketamine in esketamine responders — not the effect of starting it in an unselected patient.
cards.type: Phase 3, multicenter, double-blind, randomized-withdrawal study (SUSTAIN-1; Daly 2019, JAMA Psychiatry). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT02493868.
cards.people: 705 adults enrolled; 455 entered optimization; 297 entered the randomized maintenance phase (mean age 46.3 years; 66.3% female) — 176 in stable remission and 121 in stable response.
cards.result: Among patients who achieved stable remission, 24 (26.7%) in the esketamine and antidepressant group and 39 (45.3%) in the antidepressant and placebo group experienced relapse (log-rank P=.003, NNT 6); esketamine decreased relapse risk by 51% (HR 0.49; 95% CI 0.29–0.84, relative). Among those who achieved stable response, 16 (25.8%) versus 34 (57.6%) relapsed (log-rank P<.001, NNT 4; HR 0.30; 95% CI 0.16–0.55, relative). The most common adverse events after randomization were transient dysgeusia, vertigo, dissociation, somnolence, and dizziness (incidence 20.4%–27.0%).
cards.watchOut: Randomized-withdrawal designs enrich for responders and for patients who tolerate the drug, and withdrawal effects can masquerade as relapse — so these NNTs describe a selected population and cannot be carried back to the starting decision. Within that fence, the separation is large and consistent across both the remission and response strata.

shelves.title: Ketamine vs ECT for severe depression: noninferior where it was tested — untested where ECT is strongest
shelves.question: Head to head, is intravenous ketamine as good as electroconvulsive therapy for treatment-resistant depression — and in whom was that actually tested?
shelves.mesh: Depressive Disorder, Treatment-Resistant · Ketamine · Electroconvulsive Therapy · Humans
shelves.balance: ELEKT-D is the comparison the field waited for, done in ECT-referred patients: ketamine met noninferiority and numerically out-responded ECT (55.4% vs 41.2%), with ECT's cost showing up where it always has — memory, measurably worse at 3 weeks and recovering only gradually — and ketamine's showing up as dissociation. Quality of life ended equal. The boundary is printed, not buried: psychotic depression was excluded, and that is precisely the population where ECT's historical claim is strongest and where no modern randomized comparison exists — so the second half of the stamp grades ECT's continued primacy there as POSSIBLE, an extrapolation from older evidence, not a trial result. In the tested population, a patient who can avoid anesthesia and memory effects without giving up response has a real option. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: ELEKT-D (Anand 2023, NEJM): ketamine was noninferior to ECT in nonpsychotic treatment-resistant depression — response 55.4% vs 41.2%
cards.summary: 403 patients referred to ECT clinics for treatment-resistant major depression without psychosis , randomized to IV ketamine (0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes, twice weekly) or ECT (three times weekly) for 3 weeks, open-label. Response (≥50% fall in QIDS-SR-16): 55.4% ketamine vs 41.2% ECT — difference 14.2 points [3.9 to 24.2]; P<0.001 for noninferiority against a −10-point margin. Memory recall fell with ECT (delayed-recall T-score change −9.7 vs −0.9) and recovered gradually in follow-up; quality-of-life improvement was similar. ECT brought musculoskeletal adverse effects; ketamine brought dissociation. No deaths are reported in the record's abstract, and none are claimed here.
cards.type: Open-label, randomized, noninferiority trial (ELEKT-D; Anand 2023, NEJM), funded by PCORI. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT03113968.
cards.people: 403 patients underwent randomization at five clinical sites (200 ketamine, 203 ECT); after 38 withdrew before starting, 195 received ketamine and 170 received ECT. Responders were followed for 6 months. The record does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: A total of 55.4% of patients in the ketamine group and 41.2% in the ECT group had a response (difference, 14.2 percentage points; 95% CI 3.9 to 24.2; P<0.001 for noninferiority of ketamine to ECT). ECT was associated with a decrease in memory recall after 3 weeks (mean decrease in delayed-recall T-score −9.7 ± 1.2 vs −0.9 ± 1.1 with ketamine), with gradual recovery during follow-up. Patient-reported quality-of-life improvement was similar. ECT was associated with musculoskeletal adverse effects; ketamine with dissociation.
cards.watchOut: The fence is the population: ELEKT-D excluded psychotic depression — historically the presentation where ECT's superiority is strongest — so this trial licenses no claim there, and there is no modern randomized comparison in that group. The trial was open-label with a self-report primary outcome, and 38 randomized patients never started treatment, more of them on the ECT side — the comparison is of treatment strategies as accepted by ECT-referred patients, which is both its realism and its bias.

shelves.title: Psychedelic-assisted therapy: positive trials under a MAYBE (weak evidence) stamp — unblinding, a complete response letter, and 2024 retractions
shelves.question: Do psilocybin (for treatment-resistant depression) and MDMA-assisted therapy (for PTSD) work — and what do the blinding problem, the FDA's 2024 decision, and the retractions do to the grade?
shelves.mesh: Psilocybin · Depressive Disorder, Treatment-Resistant · N-Methyl-3,4-methylenedioxyamphetamine · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic · Humans
shelves.balance: The trial results, stated fairly: a single 25-mg psilocybin dose beat a 1-mg control on depression scores at 3 weeks (−6.6 MADRS points), and two MDMA phase-3 trials beat placebo-plus-therapy on PTSD severity with large effect sizes. The grade is MAYBE (weak evidence) anyway, for reasons printed on the cards rather than whispered: functional unblinding is near-total for both drugs, so the double-blind design cannot do its usual work and expectancy is an unmeasured co-treatment; the psilocybin effect did not persist as sustained response at 12 weeks; and the MDMA program carries an FDA complete response letter (August 2024, declining approval and requesting a further trial) plus the 2024 retraction of three phase-2 pooled analyses over data-integrity and ethics violations. Positive p-values were never the whole of evidence; this shelf is where the library says so. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Psilocybin, COMPASS phase 2 (Goodwin 2022, NEJM): a single 25-mg dose beat 1 mg on depression scores at 3 weeks — durability gone by week 12, blinding near-impossible
cards.summary: 233 adults with treatment-resistant depression randomized to a single dose of psilocybin 25 mg, 10 mg, or 1 mg (control), each with psychological support. MADRS change at week 3: −12.0 (25 mg) vs −7.9 (10 mg) vs −5.4 (1 mg) ; the 25-mg vs 1-mg difference was −6.6 [−10.2 to −2.9], P<0.001 , while 10 mg did not separate (−2.5 [−6.2 to 1.2], P=0.18). Response and remission at week 3 supported the 25-mg result, but sustained response at 12 weeks did not — the effect decayed. Adverse events occurred in 77% (headache, nausea, dizziness), and suicidal ideation or behavior or self-injury occurred in all dose groups. The record's abstract does not state the response and remission percentages, so none are carded. Functional unblinding is near-total with a psychedelic at 25 mg — patients know what they got — and expectancy is an unmeasured co-intervention in every trial on this shelf.
cards.type: Phase 2, double-blind, randomized trial (COMPASS; Goodwin 2022, NEJM). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT03775200; the record also carries EudraCT 2017-003288-36.
cards.people: 233 participants — 79 in the 25-mg group, 75 in the 10-mg group, 79 in the 1-mg group; mean baseline MADRS 32–33 in each group. The record does not print a pooled mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: Least-squares mean changes from baseline to week 3 in MADRS were −12.0 for 25 mg, −7.9 for 10 mg, and −5.4 for 1 mg; the difference between the 25-mg and 1-mg groups was −6.6 (95% CI −10.2 to −2.9; P<0.001) and between the 10-mg and 1-mg groups −2.5 (95% CI −6.2 to 1.2; P=0.18). Incidences of response and remission at 3 weeks, but not sustained response at 12 weeks, were generally supportive of the primary results for the 25-mg group. Adverse events occurred in 179 of 233 participants (77%), including headache, nausea, and dizziness. Suicidal ideation or behavior or self-injury occurred in all dose groups.
cards.watchOut: Three structural discounts, all printed: (1) functional unblinding — a 25-mg psychedelic experience cannot be mistaken for 1 mg, so the 'double-blind' label overstates the protection against expectancy effects; (2) durability — the week-3 signal did not survive as sustained response at week 12; (3) this is one phase-2 trial from one sponsor's proprietary formulation, with no comparison against any existing treatment. The suicidality events in all arms, in a treatment-resistant population, require monitoring in any future use.

cards.headline: MDMA-assisted therapy, phase 3 #1 (Mitchell 2021, Nature Medicine): positive on CAPS-5 — and the program around it later drew an FDA complete response letter and 2024 retractions of related papers
cards.summary: 90 patients with severe PTSD (including dissociative subtype, depression, substance-use history, childhood trauma) randomized to manualized therapy with MDMA or with inactive placebo, after medication washout. CAPS-5 change in completers: −24.4 (MDMA) vs −13.9 (placebo), P<0.0001, effect size d=0.91 ; functional impairment (SDS) also improved (P=0.0116). MDMA did not induce adverse events of abuse potential, suicidality, or QT prolongation in the trial. Stated on the card itself, not in a footnote: in August 2024 the FDA issued a complete response letter declining to approve MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD, and three pooled analyses of the earlier phase-2 MDMA trials were retracted in 2024 over data-integrity and ethics violations at a trial site. The retracted papers are not this trial, and this trial has not been retracted — but the program's evidence base carries both facts wherever it is carded.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-site phase 3 trial (MAPP1; Mitchell 2021, Nat Med). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT03537014.
cards.people: 90 participants with severe PTSD randomized 1:1, receiving three preparatory and nine integrative therapy sessions around the experimental sessions. The record does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: MDMA induced significant attenuation in CAPS-5 score compared with placebo (P<0.0001, d=0.91) and significantly decreased the SDS total score (P=0.0116, d=0.43). The mean change in CAPS-5 scores in participants completing treatment was −24.4 (SD 11.6) in the MDMA group and −13.9 (SD 11.5) in the placebo group. MDMA did not induce adverse events of abuse potential, suicidality, or QT prolongation.
cards.watchOut: Functional unblinding applies here with full force: MDMA's subjective effects are unmistakable, the therapists delivering the co-intervention were not meaningfully blinded, and expectancy is a plausible contributor to an effect size (d=0.91) larger than almost any psychiatric treatment achieves. The 2024 regulatory and retraction history — printed in the headline field of this card — is part of the evidence picture: the FDA's advisory process raised exactly these blinding and conduct concerns before the complete response letter.

cards.headline: MDMA-assisted therapy, phase 3 #2 (Mitchell 2023, Nature Medicine): the confirmatory trial was positive too — the FDA still declined, August 2024
cards.summary: 104 participants with moderate-to-severe PTSD (73.1% severe) randomized to MDMA-assisted therapy or placebo with identical therapy. CAPS-5 change: −23.7 vs −14.8 (P<0.001, d=0.7) ; functional impairment (SDS): −3.3 vs −2.1 (P=0.03). Severe treatment-emergent adverse events: 5 (9.4%) on MDMA vs 2 (3.9%) on placebo; there were no deaths and no serious treatment-emergent adverse events . The regulatory ending appears on the card: the FDA's complete response letter (August 2024) declined approval and requested another phase 3 trial; three phase-2 pooled-analysis papers in this program were retracted in 2024 over data-integrity/ethics violations. Two positive phase-3 trials plus a declined application is the accurate one-line summary of this program.
cards.type: Multi-site, randomized, double-blind, confirmatory phase 3 trial (MAPP2; Mitchell 2023, Nat Med). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT04077437.
cards.people: 104 participants randomized (53 MDMA-AT, 51 placebo with therapy); 26.9% moderate and 73.1% severe PTSD; 26.9% Hispanic/Latino and 33.7% identified as other than White. The record does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: Least squares mean change in CAPS-5 score was −23.7 (−26.94, −20.44) for MDMA-AT versus −14.8 (−18.28, −11.28) for placebo with therapy (P<0.001, d=0.7). LS mean change in SDS score was −3.3 versus −2.1 (P=0.03, d=0.4), assessed by blinded independent assessors. Seven participants had a severe treatment-emergent adverse event (MDMA-AT n=5 [9.4%]; placebo n=2 [3.9%]). There were no deaths or serious treatment-emergent adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A confirmatory trial that confirms — and a regulator that declines anyway — is the lesson this card exists to teach: the FDA's stated concerns (functional unblinding, expectancy, missing abuse-liability and safety data, and therapy-conduct questions sharpened by the 2024 retractions in the phase-2 literature) are methodological, and two positive trials run the same way do not answer them. Until a trial design addresses blinding and conduct head-on, this shelf's grade stays where it is.

shelves.title: Cytisine for smoking cessation: beats placebo and nicotine replacement — not yet shown varenicline's equal
shelves.question: Cytisine — a low-cost plant alkaloid used for decades in Eastern Europe — against placebo, against nicotine replacement, and against varenicline: where does it actually stand?
shelves.mesh: Smoking Cessation · Tobacco Use Disorder · Alkaloids · Azocines · Quinolizines · Varenicline · Humans
shelves.balance: Against placebo the case is consistent across eras and regimens: 8.4% vs 2.4% sustained abstinence at 12 months on the traditional 25-day course (West 2011), and 32.6% vs 7.0% at weeks 9–12 on ORCA-2's modern 12-week 3-mg regimen, with tolerability at least as good. Against nicotine replacement, the one pragmatic trial found superiority (40% vs 31% at 1 month). Against varenicline — the strongest standard — the single head-to-head trial failed to demonstrate noninferiority (11.7% vs 13.3%), which demotes 'varenicline alternative' to POSSIBLE without making cytisine a proven lesser drug. As of the sources checked for this shelf, cytisine/cytisinicline is not FDA-approved in the US; its affordability case belongs to the countries where it is licensed. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Cytisine vs placebo (West 2011, NEJM): sustained 12-month abstinence 8.4% vs 2.4% — a 6-point absolute difference
cards.summary: 740 adult smokers at a single Polish center, randomized to a 25-day cytisine course or matching placebo, both with minimal counseling. Sustained, biochemically verified abstinence at 12 months: 8.4% (31 participants) vs 2.4% (9) — difference 6.0 points [2.7 to 9.2], P=0.001 . Seven-day point prevalence at 12 months: 13.2% vs 7.3%. Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent on cytisine (difference 5.7 points [1.2 to 10.2]). (The relative ratio implied by the stated rates is about 3.5; the record does not state a relative-risk figure, so the card carries the absolute rates and their difference.)
cards.type: Single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (West 2011, NEJM). Registry verified against the record's own databank: ISRCTN37568749.
cards.people: 740 adult smokers enrolled and randomized (370 per group). The record does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: The rate of sustained 12-month abstinence was 8.4% (31 participants) in the cytisine group compared with 2.4% (9 participants) in the placebo group (difference, 6.0 percentage points; 95% CI 2.7 to 9.2; P=0.001). The 7-day point prevalence for abstinence at the 12-month follow-up was 13.2% versus 7.3% (P=0.01). Gastrointestinal adverse events were reported more frequently in the cytisine group (difference, 5.7 percentage points; 95% CI 1.2 to 10.2).
cards.watchOut: Single-center, and the absolute quit rates are low on both arms — cytisine roughly triples a small number, it does not make quitting likely. The 25-day regimen is short and the drug is inexpensive, which is the actual public-health proposition: a modest absolute effect at very low cost, in the many countries where it is licensed.

cards.headline: Cytisine vs nicotine replacement (Walker 2014, NEJM): continuous abstinence at 1 month 40% vs 31% — superiority, in a pragmatic quitline trial
cards.summary: 1,310 adult daily smokers who called the New Zealand national quitline, randomized open-label to cytisine for 25 days (mailed free) or nicotine replacement for 8 weeks (vouchers), both with low-intensity telephone support. Self-reported continuous abstinence at 1 month: 40% (264/655) vs 31% (203/655) — difference 9.3 points [4.2 to 14.5] , with cytisine also superior at 1 week, 2 months, and 6 months. Self-reported adverse events were more frequent on cytisine (288 events among 204 participants vs 174 among 134), mainly nausea, vomiting, and sleep disorders.
cards.type: Pragmatic, open-label, noninferiority trial (Walker 2014, NEJM). Registry verified against the record's own databank: ACTRN12610000590066.
cards.people: 1,310 adult daily smokers motivated to quit who called the national quitline, randomized 1:1 (655 per group). The record does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: At 1 month, continuous abstinence was reported for 40% of participants receiving cytisine (264 of 655) and 31% receiving nicotine-replacement therapy (203 of 655), a difference of 9.3 percentage points (95% CI 4.2 to 14.5). Cytisine was superior to NRT at 1 week, 2 months, and 6 months; in a prespecified subgroup analysis cytisine was superior among women and noninferior among men. Self-reported adverse events over 6 months occurred more frequently in the cytisine group (288 events among 204 participants) than the NRT group (174 among 134), primarily nausea and vomiting and sleep disorders.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and self-reported abstinence without biochemical verification of the primary outcome — the pragmatic design mirrors real quitline practice and prices in real-world adherence, at the cost of blinding. The comparison is also regimen-asymmetric: 25 days of cytisine against 8 weeks of NRT as actually supplied by voucher, which is the health-system question rather than the pharmacology question.

cards.headline: ORCA-2 (Rigotti 2023, JAMA): modern 3-mg dosing — abstinence 32.6% vs 7.0% at weeks 9–12 on the 12-week course
cards.summary: 810 US adults who smoked daily and wanted to quit, randomized to cytisinicline 3 mg three times daily for 12 weeks, for 6 weeks then placebo, or placebo throughout, all with behavioral support. Continuous abstinence, biochemically verified: 12-week course — 32.6% vs 7.0% during weeks 9–12 (OR 6.3 [3.7–11.6], relative) and 21.1% vs 4.8% during weeks 9–24 (OR 5.3 [2.8–11.1], relative) ; 6-week course — 25.3% vs 4.4% during weeks 3–6 and 8.9% vs 2.6% through week 24. Nausea, abnormal dreams, and insomnia each occurred in under 10%; 2.9% discontinued cytisinicline for adverse events; no drug-related serious adverse events. (The brief carried this trial as JAMA Internal Medicine; the record's journal is JAMA — the card follows the record.)
cards.type: Three-group, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial (ORCA-2; Rigotti 2023, JAMA), 17 US sites. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT04576949.
cards.people: 810 randomized participants (mean age 52.5 years; 54.6% female; mean 19.4 cigarettes daily); 618 (76.3%) completed the trial.
cards.result: For the 12-week course versus placebo, continuous abstinence was 32.6% vs 7.0% during weeks 9 to 12 (OR 6.3 [95% CI 3.7–11.6]; P<.001) and 21.1% vs 4.8% during weeks 9 to 24 (OR 5.3 [95% CI 2.8–11.1]; P<.001). For the 6-week course, abstinence was 25.3% vs 4.4% during weeks 3 to 6 (OR 8.0 [3.9–16.3]; P<.001) and 8.9% vs 2.6% during weeks 3 to 24 (OR 3.7 [1.5–10.2]; P=.002). Nausea, abnormal dreams, and insomnia occurred in less than 10% of each group; 16 participants (2.9%) discontinued cytisinicline because of an adverse event; no drug-related serious adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: The 12-week course holds up far better than the 6-week course after treatment ends (21.1% vs 8.9% sustained) — duration is doing real work in this trial. As of the sources checked for this shelf (Nov 2026), cytisinicline is not FDA-approved in the United States; it is licensed in a number of other countries, and the traditional European cytisine course is the 25-day taper of Cards 1 and 4, not this 3-mg regimen.

cards.headline: Cytisine vs varenicline (Courtney 2021, JAMA): noninferiority NOT demonstrated — stated first on the comparative card
cards.summary: Cytisine failed to demonstrate noninferiority to varenicline. 1,452 Australian daily smokers randomized open-label to standard cytisine (25 days) or standard varenicline (84 days), both offered telephone support. Verified 6-month continuous abstinence: 11.7% cytisine vs 13.3% varenicline — risk difference −1.62 points (one-sided 97.5% CI −5.02 to ∞); P=0.03 for noninferiority , against a 5-point margin — the interval crosses the margin, so 'at least as good' was not established, though the point estimates are close. Self-reported adverse events were less frequent on cytisine (incident rate ratio 0.88 [0.81–0.95]).
cards.type: Noninferiority, open-label randomized trial with blinded outcome assessment (Courtney 2021, JAMA). Registry from the record's own abstract: ACTRN12616001654448 (the record carries no databank entry).
cards.people: 1,452 Australian adult daily smokers (mean age 42.9 years; 51.1% women); 1,108 (76.3%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Verified 6-month continuous abstinence rates were 11.7% for cytisine and 13.3% for varenicline (risk difference −1.62% [1-sided 97.5% CI −5.02% to ∞]; P=.03 for noninferiority) against a 5% noninferiority margin — noninferiority was not demonstrated. Self-reported adverse events occurred less frequently in the cytisine group (997 events among 482 participants) than the varenicline group (1,206 among 510 participants); incident rate ratio 0.88 (95% CI 0.81–0.95; P=.002).
cards.watchOut: Not demonstrating noninferiority is not demonstrating inferiority: the confidence interval includes differences small enough to be unimportant, and the courses being compared differ in length (25 vs 84 days) as much as in molecule. What the trial settles is narrower — on this evidence a clinic cannot yet promise patients the cheaper 25-day course is varenicline's equal, and ORCA-2's longer cytisinicline regimens have not been trialed against varenicline at all.

shelves.title: Cannabis and cannabinoids for chronic pain: a small average effect, honestly sized — and harms that grow with duration
shelves.question: For chronic pain, how much do cannabis and cannabinoids actually help — in absolute terms patients can feel — and what do they cost?
shelves.mesh: Chronic Pain · Cannabinoids · Medical Marijuana · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Humans
shelves.balance: Sized honestly, the benefit is small: across 32 non-inhaled trials the average pain advantage is half a centimetre on a 10-cm scale, which translates to about 1 in 10 more patients reaching the smallest difference patients can feel — and no improvement at all in emotional, role, or social functioning (high certainty). The broadest review's responder statistic (37% vs 31%) carries a confidence interval that touches the null, and the most favorable result on the shelf — inhaled cannabis for neuropathic pain, NNT 5.6 — rests on 178 patients followed for days to weeks with unblinding built in. The harms are neither rare nor static: dizziness in 9 more patients per 100 in short trials and 28 more per 100 in trials of 3 months or longer, plus drowsiness, nausea, and cognitive effects. Follow-up across the whole literature is 1 to 5.5 months; nothing here speaks to years of use. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: The broad review (Whiting 2015, JAMA): for chronic pain, ≥30% pain reduction 37% vs 31% — OR 1.41 with an interval that touches the null
cards.summary: 79 trials, 6,462 participants, across all cannabinoid indications; the chronic-pain subset (8 trials) found a greater proportion achieving at least 30% pain reduction on cannabinoids: 37% vs 31% — OR 1.41 [0.99–2.00], relative , an interval whose lower bound sits on the null, stated as such. Average pain scores fell by WMD −0.46 points on a 0–10 scale. Short-term adverse events increased — dizziness, dry mouth, nausea, fatigue, somnolence, euphoria, disorientation, confusion, hallucination among them — including serious adverse events. Only 4 of the 79 trials were judged at low risk of bias.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Whiting 2015, JAMA) of randomized trials of cannabinoids for chronic pain, spasticity, chemotherapy nausea, and other indications. No registry ID applies to the review itself. The record does not print a pooled mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 79 trials with 6,462 participants in total; the chronic-pain responder analysis pooled 8 trials.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, cannabinoids were associated with a greater average number of patients showing reduction in pain (37% vs 31%; OR 1.41 [95% CI 0.99–2.00]; 8 trials) and a greater average reduction in numerical rating scale pain (WMD −0.46 [95% CI −0.80 to −0.11]; 6 trials). There was an increased risk of short-term adverse events with cannabinoids, including serious adverse events; common events included dizziness, dry mouth, nausea, fatigue, somnolence, euphoria, vomiting, disorientation, drowsiness, confusion, loss of balance, and hallucination. The authors graded moderate-quality evidence for chronic pain and spasticity.
cards.watchOut: The headline statistic of this shelf is an odds ratio whose confidence interval includes 1.00 — the difference between 'cannabinoids help a few more patients reach 30% relief' and 'no proven difference' is inside this review's precision. Preparations, doses, and pain conditions varied widely across the pooled trials, and psychoactive unblinding shadows every subjective pain outcome in this literature. The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Whiting PF et al. Cannabinoids for medical use: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA. 2015;313(24):2456–2473. PMID 26103030. DOI 10.1001/jama.2015.6358

cards.headline: The living review (Wang 2021, BMJ): non-inhaled cannabis — a half-centimetre of pain relief, no gain in emotional, role, or social functioning, and dizziness that compounds with duration
cards.summary: 32 randomized trials, 5,174 patients , follow-up 1 to 5.5 months; 30 oral and 2 topical preparations, 29 trials against placebo. Pain relief: WMD −0.50 cm on a 10-cm scale (moderate certainty) , with a modelled 10% more patients reaching the 1-cm minimum important difference (NNT ≈10) . Oral cannabis produced a very small improvement in physical functioning and a small improvement in sleep quality — and did not improve emotional, role, or social functioning (high certainty) . Harms per 100 patients vs placebo: dizziness +9 in trials under 3 months and +28 in trials of 3 months or longer , drowsiness +5, nausea +5, vomiting +3, transient cognitive impairment +2, impaired attention +3.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials (Wang 2021, BMJ; the evidence review behind the BMJ Rapid Recommendation). No registry ID applies to the review itself (protocol registered on OSF, as printed on the record).
cards.people: 32 trials with 5,174 adult patients — 28 in chronic non-cancer pain and 4 in cancer-related pain; follow-up ranged from 1 to 5.5 months.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, non-inhaled medical cannabis probably results in a small increase in the proportion of patients experiencing at least the minimally important difference of 1 cm in pain relief (modelled risk difference 10% [95% CI 5% to 15%]), based on a WMD of −0.50 cm (95% CI −0.75 to −0.25; moderate certainty). Oral cannabis results in a very small improvement in physical functioning (WMD 1.67 points on the 100-point SF-36; high certainty) and a small improvement in sleep quality, but does not improve emotional, role, or social functioning (high certainty). Harms (risk differences vs placebo): dizziness 9% (5% to 14%) in trials with <3 months follow-up versus 28% (18% to 43%) with ≥3 months; drowsiness 5% (2% to 8%); nausea 5% (2% to 8%); vomiting 3%; transient cognitive impairment 2%; impaired attention 3%.
cards.watchOut: Half a centimetre on a 10-cm scale is below what an individual patient can feel; the responder framing (about 1 in 10 more patients reaching the minimum important difference) is the fair way to say it, and this shelf says it both ways. The dizziness gradient by trial duration (+9 short, +28 longer) is the harm signal to carry into practice, and follow-up beyond 5.5 months does not exist in this evidence — long-term benefit and harm are both unmeasured.

cards.headline: Inhaled cannabis for neuropathic pain (Andreae 2015): short-term relief in 1 of every 5–6 treated — from five small, short trials
cards.summary: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 5 randomized trials, 178 participants with chronic neuropathic pain, followed for days to weeks. Inhaled cannabis produced short-term pain reductions with a number needed to treat of 5.6 (Bayesian 95% credible interval 3.4 to 14) — relief for roughly 1 in every 5 to 6 patients treated. The authors' own limits state with the result: few studies and participants, short follow-up, shortcomings in allocation concealment, and considerable attrition. (Responder percentages sometimes quoted for this analysis do not appear in the record, so they are not carded.)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of individual patient data (Andreae 2015, J Pain), Bayesian responder model. Protocol registered on PROSPERO (CRD42011001182), as printed on the record; no trial registry ID applies to the review itself.
cards.people: 5 randomized controlled trials, 178 participants with chronic painful neuropathy, 405 observed responses; follow-up from days to weeks.
cards.result: The pooled individual patient data provide evidence that inhaled cannabis results in short-term reductions in chronic neuropathic pain for 1 in every 5 to 6 patients treated (number needed to treat 5.6, Bayesian 95% credible interval 3.4 to 14). The Bayes factor was 332, corresponding to a posterior probability of effect of 99.7%. The authors caution that the small number of studies and participants, the short follow-up, shortcomings in allocation concealment, and considerable attrition limit the conclusions that can be drawn.
cards.watchOut: The most favorable number on this shelf comes from its weakest vessel: 178 patients, days-to-weeks of follow-up, and a treatment whose psychoactive effects unblind it — in a condition (neuropathic pain) where expectation moves scores. It is evidence that inhaled cannabis can relieve neuropathic pain briefly in some patients; it is not evidence about months, function, or safety over time, and the shelf does not stretch it. The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: Aspirin to prevent preeclampsia: the ASPRE strategy works — whether the 81 mg US dose does the same is unproven
shelves.question: Does aspirin prevent preeclampsia — and does the answer depend on the dose and the start date?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aspirin · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Incidence · Infant, Newborn · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Pre-Eclampsia · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications · Pregnancy Outcome · Risk
shelves.balance: In screened high-risk women, 150 mg nightly from the first trimester prevented about 1 case of preterm preeclampsia for every 37 treated (1.6% vs 4.3%), with no excess of adverse events — and preeclampsia is delayed/prevented disease where the word fits: this is true prevention of the preterm form, not the term form, which no dose has been shown to reduce. The dose-and-timing meta-analyses agree that dose and start date are the intervention: benefit is confined to ≥100 mg started at or before 16 weeks. The open wound is dose translation: the 81 mg dose US practice actually uses has never been shown to do the same job (Reference 3), and whether two 81 mg tablets equal the ASPRE regimen is inference, not trial evidence. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026 (Tier C — personal ruling).

cards.headline: ASPRE (Rolnik 2017, NEJM): 150 mg nightly from the first trimester — preterm preeclampsia 1.6% vs 4.3% in screened high-risk women
cards.summary: 1,776 women with singleton pregnancies, identified as high-risk for preterm preeclampsia by first-trimester combined screening, randomized to aspirin 150 mg nightly from 11–14 weeks until 36 weeks vs placebo. Preterm preeclampsia: 13 (1.6%) vs 35 (4.3%) — OR 0.38 [0.20–0.74], P=0.004 ; a 62% relative reduction and a 2.7-point absolute difference, NNT ≈37 . No significant differences in neonatal adverse outcomes or other adverse events. Re-card — this trial’s home is Shelf #151; it is counted once in the library total.
cards.type: Multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial (ASPRE). Re-card of Shelf #151 Card 2, counted once at home. The record does not print a mean age for the cohort, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 1,776 women with singleton pregnancies at high risk for preterm preeclampsia; 152 withdrew consent and 4 were lost to follow-up, leaving 798 in the aspirin group and 822 in the placebo group in the analysis.
cards.result: Preterm preeclampsia occurred in 13 participants (1.6%) in the aspirin group, as compared with 35 (4.3%) in the placebo group (odds ratio 0.38; 95% CI 0.20 to 0.74; P=0.004). Results were materially unchanged in a sensitivity analysis accounting for withdrawals and losses. Adherence was good, with a reported intake of 85% or more of the required tablets in 79.9% of participants. There were no significant between-group differences in the incidence of neonatal adverse outcomes or other adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The win is specific — screened high-risk women, 150 mg, at night, started by 14 weeks. Term preeclampsia was not the endpoint this trial moved (see Card 2). Adherence-stratified odds ratios quoted from secondary analyses of ASPRE do not appear on this record, so they are not carded here.

cards.headline: The dose-and-timing meta-analyses (Roberge 2017–2018, AJOG): benefit is confined to ≥100 mg started ≤16 weeks — and no dose reduces term preeclampsia
cards.summary: Roberge 2017 ( 45 RCTs, 20,909 women ): started ≤16 weeks, a clear dose-response — preeclampsia RR 0.57 [0.43–0.75], relative , severe preeclampsia RR 0.47, fetal growth restriction RR 0.56, higher doses doing more. Roberge 2018 ( 16 trials, 18,907 women ): the preterm-preeclampsia reduction was confined to ≥100 mg started ≤16 weeks — RR 0.33 [0.19–0.57], relative ; term preeclampsia was NOT reduced (RR 0.92 [0.70–1.21]) .
cards.type: Two systematic reviews and meta-analyses by the same group (Roberge et al., Am J Obstet Gynecol 2017 and 2018). No registry ID applies to either review itself. Neither record prints a pooled mean age or sex mix (all participants were pregnant women), so none is stated here.
cards.people: 2017 review: 45 randomized trials, 20,909 pregnant women, aspirin 50–150 mg daily. 2018 review: 16 trials, 18,907 participants with data for preterm and term preeclampsia.
cards.result: 2017: when aspirin was initiated at ≤16 weeks, there was a significant reduction with a dose-response effect for preeclampsia (relative risk 0.57; 95% CI 0.43–0.75), severe preeclampsia (0.47; 0.26–0.83), and fetal growth restriction (0.56; 0.44–0.70). Initiated after 16 weeks, the reduction in preeclampsia was smaller (0.81; 0.66–0.99) with no dose relationship, and there was no significant reduction in severe preeclampsia (0.85; 0.64–1.14) or fetal growth restriction (0.95; 0.86–1.05). 2018: aspirin reduced preterm preeclampsia (0.62; 0.45–0.87), but the reduction was confined to initiation at ≤16 weeks at a daily dose of ≥100 mg (0.33; 0.19–0.57; I²=0%); there was no significant effect on term preeclampsia (0.92; 0.70–1.21).
cards.watchOut: Timing and dose are not details — they are the intervention. A pooled estimate for initiation after 16 weeks against preterm preeclampsia specifically (RR 0.59, as quoted in the shelf’s presentation) appears in neither record, so it is not carded; what the records support is the smaller, dose-independent effect above.

cards.headline: The 81 mg problem (Demuth 2024, J Clin Med): the dose US practice actually uses has NOT been shown to prevent preterm preeclampsia
cards.summary: 11 RCTs, 13,981 women , aspirin 75–81 mg started in the first trimester vs placebo or no treatment. Pooled preterm preeclampsia (8 studies, 12,391 participants): RR 0.66 [0.27–1.62], relative — NOT significant (P=0.36) , with heavy heterogeneity ( I²=61% ). The reviewers’ conclusion: it cannot be concluded that 75–81 mg reduces preterm preeclampsia .
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials (Demuth et al., J Clin Med 2024). No registry ID applies to the review itself. The PubMed record carries no MeSH headings for this article, and it does not print a pooled mean age, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 11 randomized trials involving 13,981 participants; the pooled preterm preeclampsia analysis covered 8 studies and 12,391 participants. Five trials were at low risk of bias, one unclear, five at high risk.
cards.result: Doses of 75 to 81 mg of aspirin, compared with placebo or no treatment, were not associated with a significant reduction in preterm pre-eclampsia (relative risk 0.66; 95% CI 0.27 to 1.62; P=0.36), with significant heterogeneity across studies (I²=61%, P=0.02). The authors concluded it cannot be concluded that 75–81 mg daily reduces the risk of preterm pre-eclampsia, and that the true effect could not be properly estimated given the heterogeneity.
cards.watchOut: A non-significant pooled estimate is not proof that 81 mg does nothing — the interval runs from a large benefit to harm. It is proof that the ASPRE result has never been demonstrated at this dose. Whether two 81 mg tablets (162 mg) reproduce the trial-proven regimen is inference, not trial evidence.
