shelves.title: Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection: the flagship trial’s primary was null — the cerebral-palsy signal pooled true
shelves.question: When preterm birth is imminent, does giving the mother magnesium sulfate protect the baby’s brain?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cerebral Palsy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gestational Age · Humans · Infant Mortality · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Magnesium Sulfate · Obstetric Labor, Premature · Pregnancy · Tocolytic Agents
shelves.balance: Five trials, one direction, a consistent relative effect on cerebral palsy in survivors (RR ≈0.68, labeled relative; NNT 46 in the patient-level pooling) on a devastating outcome, at an NNT in the 40s–60s depending on baseline risk — against a cheap drug with transient maternal side effects and no excess of serious maternal harm at these doses. The honest caveats are structural, not hidden: the flagship trial’s primary endpoint was null because mortality did not move (death 9.5% vs 8.5% on BEAM), and the cerebral-palsy claim rests on a prespecified secondary endpoint in BEAM that the pooled literature then confirmed as its primary question. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: BEAM (Rouse 2008, NEJM): the primary outcome was NOT significantly different — 11.3% vs 11.7% — and that null comes first
cards.summary: 2,241 women at 24–31 weeks with imminent preterm delivery; magnesium 6 g bolus then 2 g/hour vs placebo. Primary composite (death or moderate/severe cerebral palsy): 11.3% vs 11.7% — RR 0.97 [0.77–1.23], NOT significant. The prespecified secondary analysis: moderate or severe cerebral palsy in survivors 1.9% vs 3.5% — RR 0.55 [0.32–0.95], relative; NNT 63 . Death itself did not differ ( 9.5% vs 8.5% , RR 1.12, NS). Re-card — this trial’s home is Shelf #147; it is counted once in the library total.
cards.type: Multicenter, placebo-controlled, double-blind randomized trial (BEAM). Re-card of Shelf #147, counted once at home. The record does not print a mean age for the cohort, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 2,241 women at imminent risk of delivery between 24 and 31 weeks of gestation; follow-up was achieved for 95.6% of the children.
cards.result: The rate of the primary outcome was not significantly different between the magnesium sulfate group and the placebo group (11.3% and 11.7%, respectively; relative risk 0.97; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.23). However, in a prespecified secondary analysis, moderate or severe cerebral palsy occurred significantly less frequently in the magnesium sulfate group (1.9% vs 3.5%; relative risk 0.55; 95% CI 0.32 to 0.95). The risk of death did not differ significantly between the groups (9.5% vs 8.5%; relative risk 1.12; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.47). No woman had a life-threatening event.
cards.watchOut: Read the endpoint hierarchy before the headline: BEAM missed its primary endpoint because mortality did not move. The cerebral-palsy finding is a prespecified secondary analysis — strong enough to build the pooled question on (References 2–3), not strong enough to quote BEAM alone as proof.

cards.headline: The individual-participant meta-analysis (Crowther 2017, PLoS Medicine): cerebral palsy in survivors RR 0.68 — the same effect in every cut
cards.summary: Patient-level data from all 5 trials: 5,493 women, 6,131 babies . Cerebral palsy in survivors: RR 0.68 [0.54–0.87], relative; NNT 46 . Death-or-CP combined: null overall (RR 0.94 [0.85–1.05]) but significant in the four neuroprotection-intent trials ( RR 0.86 [0.75–0.99]; NNT 41 ). Death alone: RR 1.03 — no effect .
cards.type: Individual participant data meta-analysis (Crowther et al., PLoS Medicine 2017) of the 5 eligible randomized trials. No registry ID applies to the analysis itself. The record does not print a pooled mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 5 trials, 5,493 women at risk of preterm birth and 6,131 babies; the cerebral-palsy-in-survivors analysis covered 4,601 babies.
cards.result: Overall, there was no clear effect on the primary composite of death or cerebral palsy (relative risk 0.94; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.05; 6,131 babies). In the prespecified sensitivity analysis restricted to the 4 trials with fetal-neuroprotection intent, death or CP fell significantly (RR 0.86; 0.75 to 0.99; 4,448 babies; number needed to treat 41). For cerebral palsy in survivors, magnesium had a strong protective effect overall (RR 0.68; 0.54 to 0.87; NNT to benefit 46) and in the neuroprotection-intent trials (RR 0.68; NNT 42). No effect was seen for death overall (RR 1.03; 0.91 to 1.17). The treatment effect varied little by the reason the woman was at risk of preterm birth, gestational age at treatment, total dose received, or whether maintenance therapy was used.
cards.watchOut: The load-bearing number is a relative effect on survivors — magnesium’s benefit is brain protection, not survival, and death is printed beside it on this card for that reason. Not all trials could provide every planned analysis, and low event rates limited power for some outcomes.

Paediatric mortality: RR 1.04 — no effect . Minor maternal side effects were more common; no significant effect on major maternal complications .
cards.type: Systematic review (Doyle et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2009). No registry ID applies to the review itself. The record does not print a pooled mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 5 randomized trials, 6,145 babies of women at risk of preterm birth (less than 37 weeks).
cards.result: Antenatal magnesium sulphate substantially reduced the risk of cerebral palsy in the child (relative risk 0.68; 95% CI 0.54 to 0.87; five trials; 6,145 infants) and of substantial gross motor dysfunction (RR 0.61; 0.44 to 0.85). The number of women needed to treat to benefit one baby by avoiding cerebral palsy was 63 (95% CI 43 to 87). No statistically significant effect was detected on paediatric mortality (RR 1.04; 0.92 to 1.17). There were higher rates of minor maternal side effects in the magnesium groups, but no significant effects on major maternal complications.
cards.watchOut: Every positive trial gave magnesium when birth was expected soon, and regimens varied (BEAM used a 6 g bolus, then 2 g/hour); the patient-level pooling on Card 2 found the effect similar across doses and regimens, so this shelf does not crown one regimen. The endpoint is cerebral palsy in early childhood — nothing here speaks to subtler school-age outcomes.

shelves.title: Antenatal steroids beyond 34 weeks: a late-preterm benefit with a hypoglycemia bill — and a smaller trade before term cesarean
shelves.question: Steroids before 34 weeks are settled medicine. Does extending the window — late preterm, or before a planned term cesarean — help babies or just expose them?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Betamethasone · Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia · Female · Premature Rupture of Fetal Membranes · Gestational Age · Glucocorticoids · Humans · Hypoglycemia · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Infant, Premature, Diseases · Injections, Intramuscular · Obstetric Labor, Premature · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Trimester, Third · Pulmonary Surfactants · Respiration, Artificial · Respiratory Tract Diseases
shelves.balance: Two different trades. Late preterm (ALPS): a solid, blinded trial — one severe respiratory complication prevented per 25 treated, paid for with one extra case of neonatal hypoglycemia per ~11 babies exposed (24.0% vs 15.0%); whether that hypoglycemia has any lasting consequence is unproven either way, and the trial was not built to answer childhood outcomes. There were no deaths in the 72-hour window in either arm, so the composite is about respiratory support, not survival. Term cesarean (ASTECS): a real relative effect in one open-label trial, small absolute stakes (11 vs 24 babies), and a competing intervention — delaying the cesarean to 39 weeks — that the trial’s own authors conclude also reduces these admissions, with no drug at all. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: ALPS (Gyamfi-Bannerman 2016, NEJM): late-preterm betamethasone cut respiratory complications — and raised neonatal hypoglycemia, shown on the same card
cards.summary: 2,831 women with singletons at 34 0/7–36 5/7 weeks at high risk of late-preterm delivery; betamethasone 12 mg ×2 vs placebo. Primary composite (respiratory support in the first 72 hours, stillbirth, or death): 11.6% vs 14.4% — RR 0.80 [0.66–0.97], relative; NNT 35 . Severe respiratory complications: 8.1% vs 12.1% — RR 0.67; NNT 25 . The trade: neonatal hypoglycemia 24.0% vs 15.0% — RR 1.60 [1.37–1.87]; NNH ≈11 . There were no deaths in the 72-hour window in either arm.
cards.type: Multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (ALPS). The record does not print a mean age for the cohort, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 2,831 women with a singleton pregnancy at 34 weeks 0 days to 36 weeks 5 days of gestation who were at high risk for delivery during the late preterm period; primary-outcome data for 1,427 infants in the betamethasone group and 1,400 in the placebo group.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 165 of 1,427 infants (11.6%) in the betamethasone group and 202 of 1,400 (14.4%) in the placebo group (relative risk 0.80; 95% CI 0.66 to 0.97; P=0.02). Severe respiratory complications occurred in 8.1% vs 12.1% (relative risk 0.67; 95% CI 0.53 to 0.84 — figures from the trial’s full text; number needed to treat 25). Transient tachypnea of the newborn, surfactant use, and bronchopulmonary dysplasia also occurred significantly less frequently in the betamethasone group. There were no significant differences in chorioamnionitis or neonatal sepsis. cards.headline: ASTECS (Stutchfield 2005, BMJ): steroids before term elective cesarean halved special-care admissions for respiratory distress — 11 vs 24 babies
cards.summary: 998 women booked for elective cesarean at term (≥37 weeks); two 12 mg betamethasone doses in the 48 hours before delivery vs usual care — a pragmatic, unblinded trial. Admission to special care with respiratory distress: 2.4% vs 5.1% — RR 0.46 [0.23–0.93], relative , but the absolute numbers are small ( 11 vs 24 babies ). TTN and RDS individually were not significant . The authors’ conclusion: betamethasone and delaying delivery until 39 weeks both reduce these admissions.
cards.type: Multicentre pragmatic randomised trial (ASTECS), open-label. No registry ID on record. The record does not print a mean age for the cohort, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 998 consenting women randomised at the decision to deliver by elective caesarean section at term, at 10 maternity units; 503 randomised to the treatment group.
cards.result: Of the 35 babies admitted to special baby units with respiratory distress, 24 were in the control group and 11 in the intervention group (P=0.02). The incidence of admission with respiratory distress was 0.051 in the control group and 0.024 in the treatment group (relative risk 0.46, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.93). cards.watchOut: A real relative effect in one unblinded trial on small absolute numbers — and a competing non-drug lever, waiting until 39 weeks, that does part of the same job. shelves.title: Delayed cord clamping and preterm survival: the biggest trial’s composite was null — the pooled deaths say wait
shelves.question: Does waiting at least a minute before clamping the cord save preterm babies’ lives?
shelves.mesh: Apgar Score · Constriction · Delivery, Obstetric · Female · Hematocrit · Humans · Incidence · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Infant, Premature, Diseases · Male · Perinatal Mortality · Placental Circulation · Pregnancy · Time Factors · Umbilical Cord
shelves.balance: The pooled patient-level evidence says waiting a minute or more reduces preterm death before discharge by roughly a third in relative terms (OR 0.68, high-certainty in the authors’ grading), at zero cost and with no maternal harm signal — one of the cheapest mortality interventions in medicine. The counterweight is honest and specific: the one trial large enough to answer alone (APTS) hit its composite of death or major morbidity dead level (37.0% vs 37.2%), and its mortality gap (6.4% vs 9.0%) does not survive adjustment for the many secondary outcomes examined (P=0.39 adjusted vs P=0.03 unadjusted — both printed on Card 1). The claim stands on the consistency of 48 trials, not on any single one. Cord milking is not a substitute: it showed no clear difference from immediate clamping. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026 (Tier C — personal ruling).

cards.headline: APTS (Tarnow-Mordi 2017, NEJM): the primary outcome was NULL — 37.0% vs 37.2% — the null comes first
cards.summary: 1,566 babies born before 30 weeks; clamping delayed ≥60 seconds vs immediate (≤10 seconds). Primary outcome (death or major morbidity by 36 weeks): 37.0% vs 37.2% — RR 1.00 [0.88–1.13], P=0.96. Mortality alone: 6.4% vs 9.0% — significant unadjusted ( P=0.03 ) but P=0.39 after post-hoc adjustment for multiple secondary outcomes . Both P values are shown.
cards.type: Randomized trial (APTS), intention-to-treat, accounting for multiple births. The record does not print a mean age (participants were newborns), and no pooled demographic statement applies.
cards.people: Of 1,634 fetuses randomized, 1,566 were born alive before 30 weeks of gestation (782 assigned to immediate clamping, 784 to delayed); complete data on the primary outcome for 1,497 infants (95.6%). Median time to clamping was 5 seconds vs 60 seconds.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in the incidence of the primary outcome between infants assigned to delayed clamping (37.0%) and those assigned to immediate clamping (37.2%) (relative risk 1.00; 95% CI 0.88 to 1.13; P=0.96). Mortality was 6.4% in the delayed-clamping group and 9.0% in the immediate-clamping group (P=0.03 in unadjusted analyses; P=0.39 after post hoc adjustment for multiple secondary outcomes). There were no significant differences between the groups in chronic lung disease or other major morbidities.
cards.watchOut: In the biggest trial ever done on this question, the survival difference is real in the raw numbers and fragile under multiplicity correction — a relative risk for mortality is not printed on this record, so none is carded. The shelf’s claim rests on the pooled evidence on Cards 2–3, not on APTS alone.

cards.headline: How long — and what is NOT the same intervention (Seidler 2023, Lancet network analysis): deferral ≥2 minutes carried the largest effect; cord milking is not equivalent
cards.summary: Network analysis of 47 trials, 6,094 infants : long deferral (≥120 s) reduced death before discharge the most vs immediate clamping — OR 0.31 [95% CrI 0.11–0.80], relative; moderate certainty . Cord milking vs immediate clamping: OR 0.73 [0.44–1.20] — no clear difference , low certainty; milking vs deferred clamping was likewise a wash (OR 0.95).
cards.type: Systematic review and individual participant data network meta-analysis (Seidler et al., The Lancet 2023), Bayesian random-effects; registered with PROSPERO, CRD42019136640 (as printed on the record).
cards.people: 47 trials with 6,094 participants, preterm infants; interventions grouped into immediate clamping, short deferral (≥15 s to <45 s), medium deferral (≥45 s to <120 s), long deferral (≥120 s), and intact cord milking.
cards.result: Of all interventions, long deferral reduced death before discharge the most (compared with immediate clamping; odds ratio 0.31 [95% credibility interval 0.11–0.80]; moderate certainty). Heterogeneity was low, with no indication of inconsistency. From the companion analysis (Card 2’s record): for umbilical cord milking compared with immediate clamping, no clear evidence was found of a difference in death before discharge (OR 0.73 [0.44–1.20], low certainty, 18 studies, 74 deaths); milking compared with deferred clamping likewise showed no clear difference (OR 0.95 [0.59–1.53], low certainty).
cards.watchOut: The authors’ own caveat prints with the result: in infants assessed as requiring immediate resuscitation, the long-deferral finding might only be generalisable if there are provisions for such care with the cord intact. And milking is a different intervention — a unit that substitutes milking for waiting is not delivering what the evidence supports.

shelves.title: Uterotonics compared: carbetocin is oxytocin’s equal where the fridge fails — combinations win at 500 mL, not at 1,000
shelves.question: Oxytocin is the standard for preventing postpartum hemorrhage — is anything better, and does heat-stable carbetocin earn its place where the cold chain fails?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Drug Stability · Female · Humans · Injections, Intramuscular · Oxytocics · Oxytocin · Postpartum Hemorrhage · Pregnancy · Risk · Young Adult
shelves.balance: For routine prevention: oxytocin, or heat-stable carbetocin where the fridge can’t be trusted — a genuine equal at the ≥500 mL outcome (14.5% vs 14.4%), with the ≥1,000 mL proof incomplete (noninferiority not shown, on low event rates). For high-risk women, adding misoprostol to oxytocin prevents more moderate hemorrhages (RR 0.70, relative) and roughly halves additional-uterotonic use, but no regimen has beaten oxytocin at preventing severe hemorrhage, and the extra efficacy at ≥500 mL is bought with side effects — more nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and fever. Nobody should read the combination rankings as a severe-hemorrhage claim. Postpartum hemorrhage is the leading cause of maternal death worldwide (Card 2’s record); this shelf grades prevention regimens, and prints the severe-hemorrhage outcome beside every moderate-hemorrhage claim. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026 — single grade, LIKELY, by the developer’s ruling.

cards.headline: CHAMPION (Widmer 2018, NEJM): heat-stable carbetocin was noninferior to oxytocin at ≥500 mL — and noninferiority was NOT shown at ≥1,000 mL
cards.summary: 29,645 women after vaginal birth, 23 sites in 10 countries; heat-stable carbetocin 100 µg IM vs oxytocin 10 IU IM. First primary (blood loss ≥500 mL or additional uterotonics): 14.5% vs 14.4% — RR 1.01 [0.95–1.06], relative; noninferiority shown (margin 1.16). Second primary (blood loss ≥1,000 mL): 1.51% vs 1.45% — RR 1.04 [0.87–1.25]; noninferiority NOT shown (margin 1.23 crossed; low event rates limited power). No differences in rescue interventions or adverse effects.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, noninferiority trial (CHAMPION). The record does not print a mean age for the cohort, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 29,645 women underwent randomization at 23 sites in 10 countries, after vaginal birth.
cards.result: The frequency of blood loss of at least 500 ml or the use of additional uterotonic agents was 14.5% in the carbetocin group and 14.4% in the oxytocin group (relative risk 1.01; 95% CI 0.95 to 1.06), a finding consistent with noninferiority. The frequency of blood loss of at least 1000 ml was 1.51% in the carbetocin group and 1.45% in the oxytocin group (relative risk 1.04; 95% CI 0.87 to 1.25), with the confidence interval crossing the margin of noninferiority. The use of additional uterotonic agents, interventions to stop bleeding, and adverse effects did not differ significantly between the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The design caveat prints on the card: to preserve blinding, both drugs were kept in cold storage (2 to 8°C) — so the trial proves the molecule equals oxytocin under ideal storage; the heat-stability advantage itself was never the tested variable. At ≥1,000 mL — the hemorrhage that kills — the proof is incomplete.

cards.headline: The Cochrane network meta-analysis (Gallos, 2025 update): two combinations beat oxytocin at ≥500 mL — at ≥1,000 mL, none does
cards.summary: 122 trials, 121,931 women. Against oxytocin for hemorrhage ≥500 mL: ergometrine + oxytocin RR 0.76 [0.64–0.90], relative (high certainty) and misoprostol + oxytocin RR 0.70 [0.57–0.87], relative (moderate certainty) ; carbetocin is similar to oxytocin. But at ≥1,000 mL — the hemorrhage that kills — the combinations make little or no difference vs oxytocin, and misoprostol alone may be worse (RR 1.24 [1.06–1.46]) . The combinations also bring more vomiting, diarrhea, and fever; ergometrine regimens more nausea, vomiting, and possibly hypertension.
cards.type: Network meta-analysis (Gallos et al., Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2025 update incorporating trustworthiness screening of eligible trials). No registry ID applies to the review itself (Cochrane review CD011689). The record does not print a pooled mean age or sex mix (all participants were women giving birth), so none is stated here.
cards.people: 122 trials, 121,931 women, involving seven uterotonic agents and placebo or no treatment, across 48 high-, middle- and low-income countries; most in hospital settings (94%), most with vaginal birth (71%).
cards.result: Compared with oxytocin, ergometrine plus oxytocin reduces PPH ≥500 mL (risk ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.90, high-certainty evidence), and misoprostol plus oxytocin probably reduces PPH ≥500 mL (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.87; moderate-certainty evidence). Carbetocin has similar effects compared with oxytocin. Compared with oxytocin for PPH ≥1000 mL, carbetocin and misoprostol plus oxytocin make little or no difference, and misoprostol may be less effective (RR 1.24, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.46; low-certainty evidence). Misoprostol plus oxytocin probably reduces the use of additional uterotonics (RR 0.55) and the risk of blood transfusion (RR 0.40). All uterotonic agents except carbetocin were associated with increased risks of some side effects compared with oxytocin: misoprostol may increase nausea, vomiting and fever and probably increases diarrhoea; ergometrine probably increases nausea and vomiting and may increase hypertension; the combinations increase nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, and misoprostol plus oxytocin may increase fever.
cards.watchOut: The rankings are a ≥500 mL story. At the severe-hemorrhage threshold the combinations’ advantage disappears — and postpartum haemorrhage is the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide, which is why this card prints both thresholds side by side and the shelf forbids reading the combination rankings as a severe-hemorrhage claim.

cards.headline: Why carbetocin exists at all (Lambert 2020): oxytocin is heat-sensitive, and its quality degrades where the cold chain breaks
cards.summary: Review of oxytocin quality in low- and middle-income countries: oxytocin’s quality may be degraded at numerous points along the supply chain — at manufacture, and during storage and distribution where temperature control fails. The WHO/UNFPA/UNICEF joint statement (2019) recommends oxytocin be kept at 2–8 °C throughout ; cumulative heat exposure is generally not tracked and leads to degradation. Carbetocin’s claim is logistical, not pharmacological superiority .
cards.type: Review of oxytocin quality testing, stability, and supply-chain risks in low- and middle-income countries (Lambert et al., J Pharm Policy Pract 2020). No registry ID applies. The PubMed record carries no MeSH headings for this article, so none are listed here.
cards.people: Not a patient trial — a review of oxytocin quality evidence across low- and middle-income country supply chains, supporting the WHO/UNFPA/UNICEF joint statement on oxytocin cold-chain management.
cards.result: Due to the heat sensitivity of oxytocin, its quality may be degraded at numerous points along the health supply chain — at the point of manufacture (poor-quality active pharmaceutical ingredients, lack of sterile manufacturing environments, low-quality processes) and during storage and distribution, due to lack of temperature control, including cold chain at the end-user health facility. Storing oxytocin from 2 to 8 °C throughout the supply chain is important for maintaining its quality; while short temperature excursions may not harm product quality, the cumulative heat exposure is generally not tracked and leads to degradation.
cards.watchOut: This card is the shelf’s frame, not an efficacy claim: heat-stable carbetocin exists because the places with the most maternal deaths are the places where the cold chain breaks, and WHO’s 2018 recommendations added it for settings where oxytocin quality cannot be guaranteed (guideline position, attributed). Its efficacy had to be proven separately — that was CHAMPION’s job (Reference 1).

shelves.title: 17-OHPC to prevent preterm birth: the PROLONG reversal — accelerated approval is a loan, not a verdict
shelves.question: Does weekly 17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate (17-OHPC) prevent recurrent preterm birth?
shelves.mesh: 17 alpha-Hydroxyprogesterone Caproate · Adult · Birth Weight · Cerebral Hemorrhage · Double-Blind Method · Enterocolitis, Necrotizing · Female · Humans · Hydroxyprogesterones · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Obstetric Labor, Premature · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Outcome · Progesterone Congeners · Risk · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: 17-OHPC did not prevent preterm birth in the trial built to confirm it, and the episode is this library’s cleanest lesson that accelerated approval is a loan, not a verdict. (Developer’s balance line, of record.) One trial, stopped early, with a large effect bought a decade of routine use; the confirmatory trial — larger, with the same indication — found preterm birth <35 weeks at 11.0% vs 11.5% and no difference in the neonatal composite or in fetal/early infant death (1.7% vs 1.9%). The honest complication stays printed: PROLONG’s women were lower-risk and mostly outside the US, with placebo event rates far below Meis’s, so the trials disagree partly about who was studied, not only about the drug. The fence: vaginal progesterone is a different drug by a different route for a different indication — that question lives on Shelf #418, and nothing on this shelf rules on it. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Meis 2003 (NEJM): the single trial behind accelerated approval — a large effect, in a trial stopped early
cards.summary: 463 women with a prior spontaneous preterm birth; weekly 17-OHPC 250 mg IM vs placebo. Recurrent preterm delivery <37 weeks: 36.3% vs 54.9% — RR 0.66 [0.54–0.81], relative ; <35 weeks 20.6% vs 30.7%; <32 weeks 11.4% vs 19.6%. Infants had lower rates of necrotizing enterocolitis, intraventricular hemorrhage, and supplemental-oxygen need. The trial was stopped early — which inflates effects. On this single trial, the FDA granted accelerated approval (Makena, 2011) , conditional on a confirmatory trial.
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial (Meis et al., N Engl J Med 2003), 19 clinical centers. No registry ID on record — pre-registration era. The record does not print a mean age for the cohort, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 463 pregnant women with a documented history of spontaneous preterm delivery, enrolled at 16 to 20 weeks of gestation and assigned 2:1 — 310 to 17-OHPC 250 mg weekly, 153 to inert oil placebo — injections continued until delivery or 36 weeks.
cards.result: Treatment with 17P significantly reduced the risk of delivery at less than 37 weeks of gestation (incidence 36.3 percent in the progesterone group vs 54.9 percent in the placebo group; relative risk 0.66 [95% CI 0.54 to 0.81]), delivery at less than 35 weeks (20.6 percent vs 30.7 percent; relative risk 0.67 [0.48 to 0.93]), and delivery at less than 32 weeks (11.4 percent vs 19.6 percent; relative risk 0.58 [0.37 to 0.91]). Infants of women treated with 17P had significantly lower rates of necrotizing enterocolitis, intraventricular hemorrhage, and need for supplemental oxygen.
cards.watchOut: A big effect from a single trial that was stopped early — early stopping inflates effect estimates, and the placebo group’s 54.9% recurrence rate marks a particularly high-risk US cohort. The FDA’s accelerated approval (Makena, 2011) was explicitly a loan against a confirmatory trial; Card 2 is the repayment coming due.

cards.summary: 1,708 women with a prior singleton spontaneous preterm birth (1,130 on 17-OHPC, 578 on placebo), same regimen as Meis. Preterm birth <35 weeks: 11.0% vs 11.5% — RR 0.95 [0.71–1.26], NOT significant. Neonatal morbidity composite: 5.6% vs 5.0% (RR 1.12) — no difference. Fetal/early infant death: 1.7% vs 1.9% — no difference. The US subgroup was likewise null.
cards.type: Multicenter, international, randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial (PROLONG), 93 clinical centers. Journal as printed on the record: American Journal of Perinatology (the shelf’s presentation had carried a different journal name; the record governs). The record does not print a mean age, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 1,708 women with a previous singleton spontaneous preterm birth — 1,130 received 17-OHPC 250 mg IM weekly and 578 placebo, enrolled at 16 0/7 to 20 6/7 weeks, treated until delivery or 36 weeks. Overall 87% were Caucasian, 12% had more than one prior spontaneous preterm birth, and fewer than 2% had cervical shortening <25 mm; 23% were enrolled in the United States.
cards.result: There were no significant differences in the frequency of preterm birth <35 weeks (17-OHPC 11.0% vs placebo 11.5%; relative risk 0.95 [95% CI 0.71–1.26]) or neonatal morbidity index (17-OHPC 5.6% vs placebo 5.0%; relative risk 1.12 [95% CI 0.68–1.61]). There were also no differences in frequency of fetal/early infant death (17-OHPC 1.7% vs placebo 1.9%; relative risk 0.87 [0.4–1.81]). In the subgroup enrolled in the United States (n=391), rates of preterm birth <35 weeks were higher but likewise not significantly different (15.6% vs 17.6%; relative risk 0.88 [0.55–1.40]).
cards.watchOut: The honest complication, printed: PROLONG’s women were lower-risk and mostly outside the US, with placebo event rates far below Meis’s — so the trials disagree partly about who was studied, not only about the drug. But a confirmatory trial is the test the approval was conditioned on, and in the population it enrolled, the drug did not work.

shelves.title: Short cervix: vaginal progesterone vs cervical pessary — one pooled case, one unreplicated debut
shelves.question: An asymptomatic singleton pregnancy, cervix ≤25 mm at midtrimester — what actually prevents preterm birth?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravaginal · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Outcome · Premature Birth · Progesterone · Progestins · Risk · Treatment Outcome · Uterine Cervical Diseases
shelves.balance: These are not two equivalent contenders, and the shelf keeps the tension printed under the developer’s single LIKELY stamp. Progesterone’s case is five trials pooled at the patient level (974 women) with concordant neonatal benefits — preterm birth <33 weeks RR 0.62 (relative), respiratory distress syndrome RR 0.47, composite neonatal morbidity/mortality RR 0.59 — against a neonatal-death estimate too small to call (1.4% vs 3.2%, RR 0.44, NS). The pessary’s case is one unblinded trial whose headline effect (6% vs 27%) no larger trial has reproduced: the 932-woman replication found 12.0% vs 10.8%, with perinatal death 3.2% vs 2.4%. There is still no adequate head-to-head trial of the two — every “versus” in this shelf’s title is an indirect comparison, and the shelf says so. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026 — LIKELY overall, both treatments, by the developer’s ruling, overriding the split stamp proposed at presentation.

cards.headline: Vaginal progesterone, the patient-level pooling (Romero 2018, AJOG): preterm birth <33 weeks RR 0.62, with concordant neonatal benefits
cards.summary: Individual data from 5 trials, 974 women with a singleton pregnancy and cervix ≤25 mm; progesterone gel 90 mg or capsules 200 mg daily vs placebo. Preterm birth <33 weeks: RR 0.62 [0.47–0.81], relative; NNT ≈12 — and the benefit runs one way across every cut: respiratory distress syndrome RR 0.47 , composite neonatal morbidity/mortality RR 0.59 [0.38–0.91] , NICU admission reduced. Neonatal death 1.4% vs 3.2% (RR 0.44, NS — too few deaths to call). No excess maternal adverse events, anomalies, or 2-year neurodevelopmental harm.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of individual patient data (Romero et al., Am J Obstet Gynecol 2018), 2-stage analysis, GRADE-assessed. No registry ID applies to the analysis itself. The record does not print a pooled mean age, so none is stated here.
cards.people: Data from 974 women (498 allocated to vaginal progesterone, 476 to placebo) with a cervical length ≤25 mm, participating in 5 high-quality trials.
cards.result: Vaginal progesterone was associated with a significant reduction in preterm birth <33 weeks of gestation (relative risk 0.62; 95% CI 0.47–0.81; P=.0006; high-quality evidence; control-group risk 225 per 1,000 in the review’s GRADE summary — NNT ≈12). It also significantly decreased preterm birth <36, <35, <34, <32, <30, and <28 weeks; spontaneous preterm birth <33 and <34 weeks; respiratory distress syndrome (RR 0.47 [0.27–0.81], in the review’s full text); composite neonatal morbidity and mortality (RR 0.59 [0.38–0.91]); birthweight <1500 and <2500 g; and admission to the neonatal intensive care unit (relative risks from 0.47 to 0.82; high-quality evidence for all). There were 7 (1.4%) neonatal deaths in the progesterone group and 15 (3.2%) in the placebo group (relative risk 0.44; 95% CI 0.18–1.07; P=.07; low-quality evidence). Maternal adverse events, congenital anomalies, and adverse neurodevelopmental and health outcomes at 2 years of age did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: The tension, printed: efficacy had been questioned after the OPPTIMUM study — the largest included trial, null on its primary outcomes in a mixed high-risk population — but OPPTIMUM enrolled more than short-cervix women, and in this short-cervix population the pooled effect survives its inclusion. The neonatal-death estimate (RR 0.44) is not significant and this card does not call it.
cards.source: Romero R et al. Vaginal progesterone for preventing preterm birth and adverse perinatal outcomes in singleton gestations with a short cervix: a meta-analysis of individual patient data. Am J Obstet Gynecol. 2018;218(2):161–180. PMID 29157866. DOI 10.1016/j.ajog.2017.11.576

cards.headline: PECEP (Goya 2012, Lancet): the pessary’s spectacular debut — spontaneous preterm birth 6% vs 27%, in one unblinded trial
cards.summary: 385 women with cervix ≤25 mm at 20–23 weeks; Arabin pessary vs expectant management, open-label . Spontaneous preterm birth <34 weeks: 12 (6%) vs 51 (27%) — OR 0.18 [0.08–0.37], relative; P<0.0001 . No serious adverse effects associated with the pessary were reported. An effect that large, in one unblinded trial, is exactly the shape that demands replication before belief — Card 3 is the replication.
cards.type: Randomised, controlled, open-label trial (PECEP), five hospitals in Spain. Not masked — the nature of the intervention made masking impossible. The record prints the participants’ age range (18–43 years) rather than a mean, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 385 pregnant women with a cervical length of 25 mm or less were assigned to the pessary (n=192) or expectant management (n=193); 190 were analysed in each group.
cards.result: Spontaneous delivery before 34 weeks of gestation was significantly less frequent in the pessary group than in the expectant management group (12 [6%] vs 51 [27%]; odds ratio 0.18, 95% CI 0.08–0.37; P<0.0001). No serious adverse effects associated with the use of a cervical pessary were reported.
cards.watchOut: An odds ratio of 0.18 for a silicone ring is almost unheard of in obstetrics — and it comes from a single, unblinded trial. Spectacular first results in unblindable interventions are precisely the ones replication exists for. Card 3 is that replication, and it found nothing.

cards.headline: The replication (Nicolaides 2016, NEJM): no significant difference — spontaneous birth <34 weeks 12.0% vs 10.8%
cards.summary: 932 women with singleton pregnancies and cervix ≤25 mm; pessary vs expectant management. Spontaneous birth <34 weeks: 12.0% vs 10.8% — OR 1.12 [0.75–1.69], relative; P=0.57 — NULL. Perinatal death: 3.2% vs 2.4% (P=0.42); adverse neonatal outcome and neonatal special care likewise did not differ. Vaginal discharge was significantly more common with the pessary.
cards.type: Multicenter, randomized, controlled trial (Nicolaides et al., N Engl J Med 2016), intention-to-treat. The record does not print a mean age for the cohort, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 932 girls and women with singleton pregnancies and a cervical length of 25 mm or less at 20 weeks 0 days to 24 weeks 6 days of gestation — 465 assigned to pessary placement and 467 to expectant management. Participants in either group with a cervical length of 15 mm or less received vaginal progesterone.
cards.result: There was no significant difference between the pessary group and the control group in spontaneous delivery before 34 weeks (12.0% and 10.8%, respectively; odds ratio 1.12; 95% CI 0.75 to 1.69; P=0.57). There were no significant differences in the rates of perinatal death (3.2% in the pessary group and 2.4% in the control group, P=0.42), adverse neonatal outcome (6.7% and 5.7%, respectively; P=0.55), or neonatal special care (11.6% and 12.9%, respectively; P=0.59). The incidence of new or increased vaginal discharge was significantly higher in the pessary group.
cards.watchOut: One design difference gets its line: Nicolaides added progesterone when the cervix was ≤15 mm and PECEP did not — but that biases toward finding a pessary effect on top of progesterone, not against it. With the larger, later trial null, the pessary’s evidence rests on one unblinded debut; FIGO’s recommendation keeps pessaries in research settings (guideline position, attributed). The shelf carries the developer’s single LIKELY stamp over both treatments with this tension printed in full, as ruled.

shelves.title: Antibiotics for preterm rupture of membranes — and for preterm labor with intact membranes (ORACLE): one question where they help, one where the children paid
shelves.question: When labor threatens early, do broad-spectrum antibiotics help the baby — and does the answer flip when the membranes are still intact?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Amoxicillin-Potassium Clavulanate Combination · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Cerebral Palsy · Enterocolitis, Necrotizing · Erythromycin · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Obstetric Labor, Premature · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Outcome · Premature Rupture of Fetal Membranes · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: These are two different clinical questions sharing one shelf, and the fence between them is the shelf’s whole point. With ruptured membranes (ORACLE I, Card 1), erythromycin prolonged pregnancy and improved a run of short-term neonatal outcomes — the primary composite reached significance in singletons (11.2% vs 14.4%, P=0.02) though not in all infants (12.7% vs 15.2%, P=0.08) — and the 7-year follow-up (Reference 2) found no childhood penalty. Co-amoxiclav bought no primary benefit in PPROM and significantly more necrotizing enterocolitis, so it is the drug to avoid. With intact membranes (ORACLE II, Card 3), the same drugs produced no short-term neonatal benefit at all — and at age 7 the children exposed to erythromycin carried more functional impairment and roughly double the cerebral palsy. In PPROM the trade favors a macrolide; with intact membranes there is no short-term benefit to weigh against the long-term signal. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026 — split stamp LIKELY (PPROM macrolide) / POSSIBLE (intact-membrane childhood harm), as ruled.

cards.headline: ORACLE I (Kenyon 2001, Lancet): erythromycin for PPROM — the composite missed in all infants (P=0.08), hit in singletons (P=0.02); co-amoxiclav raised necrotizing enterocolitis
cards.summary: 4,826 women with preterm prelabour rupture of membranes; erythromycin 250 mg, co-amoxiclav 325 mg, both, or placebo, four times daily up to 10 days. Primary composite (neonatal death, chronic lung disease, or major cerebral abnormality), erythromycin vs placebo: all infants 12.7% vs 15.2% (P=0.08 — not significant) ; singletons 11.2% vs 14.4% (P=0.02) . Erythromycin also prolonged pregnancy and reduced surfactant use, oxygen dependence at 28 days, major cerebral abnormalities, and positive blood cultures. Co-amoxiclav: no primary benefit and significantly more neonatal necrotizing enterocolitis — the record states this qualitatively and prints no rate, so neither does this card.
cards.type: Randomised multicentre trial with a 2×2 factorial design (ORACLE I, ORACLE Collaborative Group, Lancet 2001), intention-to-treat. No registry ID appears on the record — the trial predates routine registration. The record does not print a mean age; participants were women with pPROM (MeSH: Adult).
cards.people: 4,826 women with pPROM randomly assigned 250 mg erythromycin (n=1,197), 325 mg co-amoxiclav (250 mg amoxicillin plus 125 mg clavulanic acid; n=1,212), both (n=1,192), or placebo (n=1,225), four times daily for 10 days or until delivery.
cards.result: The primary outcome was a composite of neonatal death, chronic lung disease, or major cerebral abnormality on ultrasonography before discharge from hospital. Among all 2,415 infants born to women allocated erythromycin only or placebo, fewer had the primary composite outcome in the erythromycin group (151 of 1,190 [12.7%] vs 186 of 1,225 [15.2%], P=0.08). Among the 2,260 singletons in this comparison, significantly fewer had the composite primary outcome in the erythromycin group (125 of 1,111 [11.2%] vs 166 of 1,149 [14.4%], P=0.02). Co-amoxiclav only and co-amoxiclav plus erythromycin had no benefit over placebo with regard to this outcome in all infants or in singletons only. Use of erythromycin was also associated with prolongation of pregnancy, reductions in neonatal treatment with surfactant, decreases in oxygen dependence at 28 days of age and older, fewer major cerebral abnormalities on ultrasonography before discharge, and fewer positive blood cultures. Although co-amoxiclav only and co-amoxiclav plus erythromycin were associated with prolongation of pregnancy, they were also associated with a significantly higher rate of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis.
cards.watchOut: The headline depends on which denominator you read: the all-infants comparison — the trial’s primary population — did not reach significance (P=0.08); the singleton comparison did (P=0.02). The shelf prints both, in that order. The necrotizing enterocolitis signal against co-amoxiclav is stated in the record without a rate; this card keeps it qualitative rather than borrow a number the record does not print.

cards.headline: ORACLE Children Study I (Kenyon 2008, Lancet): after PPROM, no childhood penalty at age 7 — the reassurance card
cards.summary: 3,298 children (75% of those eligible) followed to age 7 after PPROM. Functional impairment, erythromycin vs no erythromycin: 38.3% vs 40.4% — OR 0.91 [0.79–1.05], relative; not significant . Co-amoxiclav: 40.6% vs 38.1% (OR 1.11 [0.96–1.28], NS). No differences in behavioural difficulties, specific medical conditions, or school attainment in reading, writing, or mathematics. Ascertainment was by structured parent questionnaire — printed as the caveat it is.
cards.type: Prespecified 7-year follow-up of a randomised trial (ORACLE Children Study I, Lancet 2008), factorial comparisons (each antibiotic with or without the other vs none of it). No registry ID appears on the record. Outcomes were assessed with a structured parental questionnaire; functional impairment was any level (severe, moderate, or mild) on the Mark III Multi-Attribute Health Status classification system.
cards.people: Children born to the 4,148 women who had completed ORACLE I and were eligible for follow-up; outcome was determined for 3,298 (75%) eligible children at age 7 years. Educational outcomes were assessed with national curriculum test results for children resident in England.
cards.result: There was no difference in the proportion of children with any functional impairment after prescription of erythromycin, with or without co-amoxiclav, compared with those born to mothers who received no erythromycin (594 [38.3%] of 1,551 children vs 655 [40.4%] of 1,620; odds ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.79–1.05) or after prescription of co-amoxiclav, with or without erythromycin, compared with those born to mothers who received no co-amoxiclav (645 [40.6%] of 1,587 vs 604 [38.1%] of 1,584; odds ratio 1.11, 0.96–1.28). Neither antibiotic had a significant effect on the overall level of behavioural difficulties experienced, on specific medical conditions, or on the proportions of children achieving each level in reading, writing, or mathematics at key stage one.
cards.watchOut: Reassurance with its limits printed: one in four eligible children was not assessed, and health status came from a parent questionnaire, not examination. Within those limits, the PPROM exposure left no detectable childhood signal — the direct contrast with Card 3, where the membranes were intact.

cards.headline: ORACLE II + Children II (Kenyon 2001 / 2008, Lancet): intact membranes — no short-term benefit at all, and at age 7 more impairment and cerebral palsy
cards.summary: The null comes first, because it is the point: in 6,295 women in spontaneous preterm labor with intact membranes , the primary composite (neonatal death, chronic lung disease, or major cerebral abnormality) was no lower on any antibiotic than placebo — erythromycin 5.6%, co-amoxiclav 5.0%, both 5.9%, placebo 5.0% . At age 7 (3,196 children, 71% ascertained, by parent questionnaire): functional impairment on erythromycin 42.3% vs 38.3% — OR 1.18 [1.02–1.37], relative ; cerebral palsy on erythromycin 3.3% vs 1.7% — OR 1.93 [1.21–3.09], NNH 64 ; on co-amoxiclav 3.2% vs 1.9% — OR 1.69 [1.07–2.67], NNH 79 . No effect on deaths. There was no short-term benefit to weigh against any of this.
cards.type: Randomised multicentre trial with a 2×2 factorial design (ORACLE II, Lancet 2001) and its prespecified 7-year follow-up (Lancet 2008). No registry ID appears on either record. The follow-up assessed health status with a structured parental questionnaire; functional impairment was any level (severe, moderate, or mild) on the Mark III Multi-Attribute Health Status classification system. The trial record does not print a mean age (MeSH: Adult).
cards.people: ORACLE II: 6,295 women in spontaneous preterm labour with intact membranes and without evidence of clinical infection, assigned 250 mg erythromycin (n=1,611), 325 mg co-amoxiclav (n=1,550), both (n=1,565), or placebo (n=1,569), four times daily for 10 days or until delivery, whichever occurred earlier. Children Study II: children born to the 4,221 women eligible for follow-up; outcome determined for 3,196 (71%).
cards.result: Short term (ORACLE II): none of the trial antibiotics was associated with a lower rate of the composite primary outcome than placebo (erythromycin 90 [5.6%], co-amoxiclav 76 [5.0%], both antibiotics 91 [5.9%], vs placebo 78 [5.0%]). Antibiotic prescription was associated with a lower occurrence of maternal infection. At age 7 (Children Study II): a greater proportion of children whose mothers had been prescribed erythromycin, with or without co-amoxiclav, had any functional impairment than did those whose mothers had received no erythromycin (658 [42.3%] of 1,554 vs 574 [38.3%] of 1,498; odds ratio 1.18, 95% CI 1.02–1.37). Co-amoxiclav (with or without erythromycin) had no effect on functional impairment (624 [40.7%] of 1,523 vs 608 [40.0%] of 1,520; odds ratio 1.03, 0.89–1.19). More children whose mothers had received erythromycin or co-amoxiclav developed cerebral palsy than did those born to mothers who received neither, respectively (erythromycin: 53 [3.3%] of 1,611 vs 27 [1.7%] of 1,562; odds ratio 1.93, 1.21–3.09; number needed to harm 64 [37–209]; co-amoxiclav: 50 [3.2%] of 1,587 vs 30 [1.9%] of 1,586; odds ratio 1.69, 1.07–2.67; number needed to harm 79 [42–591]). No effects were seen with either antibiotic on the number of deaths, other medical conditions, behavioural patterns, or educational attainment.
cards.watchOut: The design caveats print with the signal: ascertainment was ~71% and by parent questionnaire, and cerebral palsy was not the follow-up’s primary outcome — the absolute risks stayed low (3.3% vs 1.7%). But the structure of the evidence is what earns the POSSIBLE stamp: a trial with zero short-term neonatal benefit leaves nothing on the other side of the scale, so even a moderate-certainty long-term harm signal has nothing to be weighed against.

shelves.title: Immediate kangaroo care for low-birth-weight infants: start skin-to-skin at birth, not after stabilization
shelves.question: For a baby born at 1.0–1.8 kg, does skin-to-skin care started immediately — rather than after the baby stabilizes — save lives?
shelves.mesh: Breast Feeding · Female · Humans · Infant · Infant Mortality · Infant, Low Birth Weight · Infant, Newborn · Kangaroo-Mother Care Method · Male · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: Two independent evidence layers point the same way. The older trials — kangaroo care begun mostly after stabilization, pooled by Cochrane (Reference 2) — found mortality relative risks of 0.60 at discharge and 0.67 at latest follow-up. The one large trial of the immediate strategy (iKMC, Card 1) found death by 28 days at 12.0% vs 15.7% — RR 0.75 (relative), an absolute 3.7 points, NNT ≈27 — in the low-resource settings where most of these deaths occur. The discounts are printed, not hidden: iKMC was stopped early on its monitoring board’s recommendation, which can flatter an effect; care could not be blinded; and the control group was not “no kangaroo care” but delayed kangaroo care, which if anything biases the estimate down. The claim is fenced to the studied band: infants of 1.0–1.8 kg, in hospitals able to keep mothers resident in the unit (Reference 3). Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: WHO iKMC (NEJM 2021): immediate kangaroo care — death by 28 days 12.0% vs 15.7%, RR 0.75; stopped early for benefit
cards.summary: 3,211 infants of 1.0–1.799 kg in five hospitals (Ghana, India, Malawi, Nigeria, Tanzania); immediate kangaroo care in a mother–infant unit (median 16.9 hours/day skin-to-skin) vs conventional incubator/warmer care until stable, then kangaroo care (median 1.5 hours/day). Death by 28 days: 12.0% vs 15.7% — RR 0.75 [0.64–0.89], relative; P=0.001; NNT ≈27 . The second primary, death by 72 hours, was not significant (4.6% vs 5.8%; RR 0.77 [0.58–1.04]; P=0.09). The trial was stopped early on the data and safety monitoring board’s recommendation because of the mortality difference — early stopping can flatter an effect, and the card says so. The control was delayed kangaroo care, not none.
cards.type: Randomized, controlled trial (WHO Immediate Kangaroo Mother Care Study Group, N Engl J Med 2021), five hospitals in Ghana, India, Malawi, Nigeria, and Tanzania; unblinded care. Funded by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. Registry IDs from the record’s own databank: ACTRN12618001880235 and CTRI/2018/08/015369. The record does not print a mean maternal age, so none is stated here.
cards.people: A total of 3,211 infants with a birth weight between 1.0 and 1.799 kg and their mothers were randomly assigned to the intervention group (1,609 infants with their mothers) or the control group (1,602 infants with their mothers).
cards.result: The median daily duration of skin-to-skin contact in the neonatal intensive care unit was 16.9 hours (interquartile range, 13.0 to 19.7) in the intervention group and 1.5 hours (interquartile range, 0.3 to 3.3) in the control group. Neonatal death occurred in the first 28 days in 191 infants in the intervention group (12.0%) and in 249 infants in the control group (15.7%) (relative risk of death, 0.75; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.64 to 0.89; P=0.001) — an absolute difference of 3.7 percentage points, NNT ≈27. Neonatal death in the first 72 hours of life occurred in 74 infants in the intervention group (4.6%) and in 92 infants in the control group (5.8%) (relative risk of death, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.58 to 1.04; P=0.09) — the second primary outcome, not significant. The trial was stopped early on the recommendation of the data and safety monitoring board owing to the finding of reduced mortality among infants receiving immediate kangaroo mother care.
cards.watchOut: Two discounts print on the card. First, early stopping: trials stopped at a random high can overstate the effect, so RR 0.75 is read as the optimistic end of what immediate kangaroo care does. Second, the comparison is timing, not presence: the control group received kangaroo care after stabilization (median 1.5 hours/day in the unit), so the trial estimates the value of immediate and near-continuous contact against the standard sequence — not of contact against none.

cards.headline: Cochrane (Conde-Agudelo & Díaz-Rossello 2016): the after-stabilization literature — mortality RR 0.60 at discharge, RR 0.67 at latest follow-up
cards.summary: 21 trials, 3,042 low-birth-weight infants , kangaroo care mostly begun after stabilization vs conventional care; moderate-quality evidence. Mortality at discharge: RR 0.60 [0.39–0.92], relative ; at latest follow-up RR 0.67 [0.48–0.95] . Nosocomial infection/sepsis RR 0.35 [0.22–0.54] ; severe infection/sepsis at follow-up RR 0.50 [0.36–0.69] ; hypothermia RR 0.28 [0.16–0.49] ; more exclusive breastfeeding and better weight gain.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (Conde-Agudelo & Díaz-Rossello, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016, CD002771), searches to June 30, 2016. No registry ID applies to the review itself. (A systematic review — no single age or sex mix applies.)
cards.people: Twenty-one studies, including 3,042 low-birth-weight infants, fulfilled the inclusion criteria. Nineteen studies evaluated KMC in LBW infants after stabilization, one evaluated KMC before stabilization, and one compared early-onset with late-onset KMC in relatively stable infants. Sixteen studies evaluated intermittent KMC and five evaluated continuous KMC.
cards.result: At discharge or 40 to 41 weeks’ postmenstrual age, KMC was associated with a statistically significant reduction in the risk of mortality (risk ratio [RR] 0.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.39 to 0.92; eight trials, 1,736 infants), nosocomial infection/sepsis (RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.54; five trials, 1,239 infants), and hypothermia (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.49; nine trials, 989 infants; moderate-quality evidence). At latest follow-up, KMC was associated with a significantly decreased risk of mortality (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.95; 12 trials, 2,293 infants; moderate-quality evidence) and severe infection/sepsis (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.69; eight trials, 1,463 infants; moderate-quality evidence). KMC also increased weight gain and exclusive breastfeeding at discharge or 40 to 41 weeks (RR 1.16) and any breastfeeding at discharge (RR 1.20). The authors concluded that the evidence supports the use of KMC in LBW infants as an alternative to conventional neonatal care, mainly in resource-limited settings, and that further information was required concerning early-onset continuous KMC in unstabilized or relatively stabilized infants — the question Card 1’s trial then answered.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are small and mostly from resource-limited settings, care could not be blinded, and the mortality estimate rests on eight trials for the discharge outcome — hence “moderate-quality” in the review’s own grading, and LIKELY rather than a stronger stamp on this shelf. Nineteen of the 21 studies started KMC after stabilization, so this card supports kangaroo care itself; the immediate claim rests on Card 1.

cards.headline: What the intervention actually demands: a mother–infant unit, ~17 hours a day, from the first hours — an infrastructure commitment, not advice
cards.summary: The iKMC intervention restructured the unit: mothers (or surrogates) resident in the neonatal unit delivering a median 16.9 hours/day of contact from the first hours of life, where control-group mortality was 15.7% by 28 days. WHO’s 2022 guideline recommends kangaroo care as routine care for preterm/low-birth-weight infants, started as soon as possible after birth (guideline position, attributed). The evidence below 1.0 kg and in ventilated infants is thin — the shelf fences its claim to the studied 1.0–1.8 kg band .
cards.type: Implementation frame drawn from the two records on this shelf (iKMC, PMID 34038632; Cochrane review, PMID 27552521) plus the WHO guideline position, attributed as such. No new trial evidence is claimed on this card.
cards.people: The settings of Cards 1 and 2: neonatal units — five hospitals in Ghana, India, Malawi, Nigeria, and Tanzania for iKMC — caring for infants of 1.0–1.799 kg, with mothers or surrogates able to stay resident in the unit.
cards.result: The intervention is a dose, and the dose is large: a median 16.9 hours a day of skin-to-skin contact in a mother–infant unit, against 1.5 hours a day in conventional care — a staffing, space, and family-presence commitment, not a poster on the wall. Within the Cochrane review, the single trial of early-onset (within 24 hours) versus late-onset continuous KMC in 73 relatively stable infants found no significant differences in mortality, morbidity, severe infection, hypothermia, breastfeeding, or nutritional indicators, with a shorter hospital stay on early onset (mean difference 0.9 days) — one small trial, printed at its weight; the immediate-timing claim rests on iKMC. WHO’s 2022 guideline recommends kangaroo mother care as routine care for preterm and low-birth-weight infants, started as soon as possible after birth (guideline position, attributed).
cards.watchOut: The fence: iKMC enrolled 1.0–1.799 kg infants, and neither it nor the pooled Cochrane trials establish the claim below 1.0 kg or in ventilated infants. Units where mothers cannot stay — or where baseline mortality is far lower than the trial settings’ — should expect the relative effect to travel better than the absolute 3.7 points.
cards.source: WHO Immediate Kangaroo Mother Care Study Group. N Engl J Med. 2021;384(21):2028–2038. PMID 34038632 · Conde-Agudelo A, Díaz-Rossello JL. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2016;(8):CD002771. PMID 27552521 · WHO guideline on care of the preterm and low-birth-weight infant (2022), guideline position as attributed

shelves.title: CPAP first vs early surfactant in extremely preterm infants: start noninvasive, ventilate selectively
shelves.question: For a baby born at 24–28 weeks, should the default be a tube and surfactant in the first hour, or CPAP in the delivery room with surfactant only if needed?
shelves.mesh: Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Intubation, Intratracheal · Male · Pneumothorax · Pulmonary Surfactants · Respiration, Artificial
shelves.balance: No individual trial won its primary endpoint — SUPPORT’s death-or-BPD composite was 47.8% vs 51.0% (RR 0.95, NS) and COIN’s was OR 0.80 (NS) — and this shelf prints those nulls first, because they are the honest headline. What CPAP-first bought, consistently, was exposure: fewer intubations, fewer ventilator days, roughly half the surfactant, and less postnatal steroid use, at no measured cost in death, BPD, or 18–22-month neurodevelopment (SUPPORT follow-up: death or impairment 27.9% vs 29.9%, NS). Pooled across the avoidance-of-ventilation trials, death or BPD does reach significance (OR 0.83, NNT 35 — Card 3, with the record’s own numbers). The price on the ledger is COIN’s pneumothorax signal (9% vs 3%), from the highest-pressure CPAP strategy in the set and not reproduced in SUPPORT. Nothing here says surfactant is obsolete — nearly half of CPAP-first babies receive it anyway; what changed is the default order. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: SUPPORT (Finer 2010, NEJM): the null printed first — death or BPD 47.8% vs 51.0%, RR 0.95, not significant
cards.summary: 1,316 infants at 24 0/7–27 6/7 weeks; delivery-room CPAP with a limited-ventilation strategy vs intubation + surfactant within 1 hour. Primary outcome, death or BPD at 36 weeks (physiologic definition): 47.8% vs 51.0% — RR 0.95 [0.85–1.05], relative; NOT significant ; by the any-oxygen definition 48.7% vs 54.1% (RR 0.91 [0.83–1.01]). The CPAP group’s wins are in exposure: less intubation and fewer postnatal corticosteroids for BPD (both P<0.001), fewer ventilator days (P=0.03), more infants alive and off the ventilator by day 7 (P=0.01). At 18–22 months, death or neurodevelopmental impairment did not differ: 27.9% vs 29.9% (RR 0.93 [0.78–1.10]; P=0.38).
cards.type: Randomized, multicenter trial with a 2-by-2 factorial design (SUPPORT — Surfactant, Positive Pressure, and Oxygenation Randomized Trial; Finer et al., N Engl J Med 2010); infants were also randomized to one of two oxygen-saturation target ranges. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT00233324. The record does not print a mean gestational age beyond the eligibility range, so none is stated here.
cards.people: A total of 1,316 infants born between 24 weeks 0 days and 27 weeks 6 days of gestation, randomly assigned to intubation and surfactant treatment (within 1 hour after birth) or to CPAP treatment initiated in the delivery room, with subsequent use of a protocol-driven limited ventilation strategy.
cards.result: The rates of the primary outcome did not differ significantly between the CPAP group and the surfactant group (47.8% and 51.0%, respectively; relative risk with CPAP, 0.95; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.85 to 1.05) after adjustment for gestational age, center, and familial clustering. The results were similar when bronchopulmonary dysplasia was defined according to the need for any supplemental oxygen at 36 weeks (rates of primary outcome, 48.7% and 54.1%, respectively; relative risk with CPAP, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.83 to 1.01). Infants who received CPAP treatment, as compared with infants who received surfactant treatment, less frequently required intubation or postnatal corticosteroids for bronchopulmonary dysplasia (P<0.001 for both comparisons), required fewer days of mechanical ventilation (P=0.03), and were more likely to be alive and free from the need for mechanical ventilation by day 7 (P=0.01). The rates of other adverse neonatal outcomes did not differ significantly between the two groups. Longer-term follow-up (Vaucher et al., N Engl J Med 2012; PMID 23268664): the primary outcome was determined for 1,234 of 1,316 enrolled infants (93.8%); death or neurodevelopmental impairment at 18 to 22 months of corrected age occurred in 27.9% of the infants in the CPAP group (173 of 621) versus 29.9% of those in the surfactant group (183 of 613) (relative risk, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.78 to 1.10; P=0.38).
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome is a null, and the shelf’s claim is built accordingly: CPAP-first is supported as an alternative default that reduces exposure to intubation, ventilation, and steroids — not as a strategy proven to cut death or BPD in this trial. The two oxygen-saturation arms are the trial’s other factorial half; their results are a separate question and are not this card’s claim.

cards.headline: COIN (Morley 2008, NEJM): the same NS trend — and the harm card: pneumothorax 9% vs 3% on the higher-pressure CPAP strategy
cards.summary: 610 infants at 25–28 weeks, breathing at 5 minutes; nasal CPAP at 8 cm water vs intubation. Death or BPD at 36 weeks: 33.9% vs 38.9% — OR 0.80 [0.58–1.12], relative; P=0.19, not significant ; death or oxygen at 28 days favored CPAP (OR 0.63 [0.46–0.88]; P=0.006), with little difference in overall mortality . The harm: pneumothorax 9% vs 3% (P<0.001) . In the CPAP group, 46% were still intubated during the first 5 days and surfactant use was halved — CPAP-first is selective escalation, not CPAP instead of everything. Fewer ventilator days.
cards.type: Randomized trial (COIN — CPAP Or Intubation trial; Morley et al., N Engl J Med 2008). Registry number as printed in the record: Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry 12606000258550 (ACTRN12606000258550). The record does not print a mean gestational age beyond the eligibility range, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 610 infants born at 25-to-28-weeks’ gestation who were breathing at 5 minutes after birth — 307 assigned to CPAP and 303 to intubation in the 36-week analysis.
cards.result: At 36 weeks’ gestational age, 33.9% of 307 infants who were assigned to receive CPAP had died or had bronchopulmonary dysplasia, as compared with 38.9% of 303 infants who were assigned to receive intubation (odds ratio favoring CPAP, 0.80; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.58 to 1.12; P=0.19). At 28 days, there was a lower risk of death or need for oxygen therapy in the CPAP group than in the intubation group (odds ratio, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.46 to 0.88; P=0.006). There was little difference in overall mortality. In the CPAP group, 46% of infants were intubated during the first 5 days, and the use of surfactant was halved. The incidence of pneumothorax was 9% in the CPAP group, as compared with 3% in the intubation group (P<0.001). There were no other serious adverse events. The CPAP group had fewer days of ventilation.
cards.watchOut: The pneumothorax signal is this shelf’s harm, and its context prints with it: COIN used CPAP at 8 cm water from 5 minutes of life — the most aggressive pressure strategy among the major trials — and SUPPORT, with a gentler delivery-room approach, did not report a pneumothorax excess among its adverse outcomes. The signal is read as pressure-dependent, not as a verdict on CPAP-first itself; units adopting the strategy inherit the duty to watch air leak.

cards.headline: The pooled answer (Fischer & Bührer 2013, Pediatrics): death or BPD OR 0.83 [0.71–0.96], NNT 35 — across 7 trials, no one of which won alone
cards.summary: 7 trials, 3,289 infants under 30 weeks, pooling strategies to avoid endotracheal ventilation (delivery-room CPAP chief among them) vs earlier intubation. Death or BPD: OR 0.83 [0.71–0.96], relative; NNT 35 — the record’s own odds ratio and NNT. Results were remarkably homogeneous; no influence on severe intraventricular hemorrhage. No individual trial won its primary endpoint; the pooled estimate crosses significance because the trials leaned the same way.
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (Fischer & Bührer, Pediatrics 2013), using the standard methods of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group; trials published since 2000, searches to February 2013. No registry ID applies to the analysis itself. (A meta-analysis — no single age or sex mix applies.)
cards.people: Seven trials including a total of 3,289 preterm infants <30 weeks’ gestational age, comparing a strategy aimed at avoiding endotracheal mechanical ventilation with a control group in which mechanical ventilation via an endotracheal tube was performed at an earlier stage.
cards.result: The combined odds ratio (95% confidence interval) of death or BPD was 0.83 (0.71–0.96). The number needed to treat was 35. The study results were remarkably homogeneous. Avoiding endotracheal ventilation had no influence on the incidence of severe intraventricular hemorrhage. The authors concluded that strategies aimed at avoiding endotracheal ventilation in infants <30 weeks’ gestational age have a small but significant beneficial impact on preventing BPD.
cards.watchOut: Scope, printed: the pooled set is broader than “CPAP vs surfactant” alone — it pools strategies for avoiding endotracheal ventilation, of which delivery-room CPAP is the main one — and the pooled claim is about the composite of death or BPD, driven substantially by BPD. The effect is real but small (NNT 35): this card supports the default order, not a transformation of outcomes.
